mechaber/1:main: The law of wheat upon which water fell, and a cooked dish in which wheat was found. And in it are 16 seifim: Grain that was submerged in a river or upon which water fell — just as it is forbidden to eat it, so it is forbidden to keep it; rather one sells it to a Jew and informs him so that he eats it before Pesach. And if he sold it to a gentile before Pesach, he sells a little to each one so that it is consumed before Pesach, lest the gentile return and sell it to a Jew:
mechaber/2:main: This grain that drowned in a river or had water fall on it, even though it did not split, is forbidden. Dachion Diminah I will leave it to the pickle: Hega, therefore, one must be careful that water or rain does not fall on the sheaves because then it is not forbidden to split. Tamtzi say go down lest we miss out, but eating them on Pesach is forbidden and not fun.
mechaber/3:main: Wheat that came in a ship — if it is dry and hard and its appearance did not change, we do not establish presumptive prohibition upon it:
mechaber/4:main: In a year when rains were abundant and descended upon heaps in the fields until some of the sheaves atop the heaps sprouted vegetation — we are not concerned about ordinary wheat of that year:
mechaber/5:main: Grain that is attached, which dried completely and does not require suckling — is considered as one who rests in a barrel and accepts chametzing if rain descends upon it:
mechaber/6:main: Wheat in which split kernels were found — those that are not split open are permitted, because it is common that at the time of rains the top of the stack chametzs and splits open and the bottom of it chametzs and splits open, and the water does not touch its middle at all:
mechaber/7:main: A Jew who has pits full of wheat and is concerned lest there be split wheat in the floor of the pit and its walls from the moisture of the pit and the earth — generic nullification suffices: (and see above siman 436 seif 1):
mechaber/8:main: Honey of a gentile — we do not establish presumptive prohibition upon it, and we eat it on Pesach: {Rama: However some are stringent (Mordechai chapter Kol Sha'ah and Hagahot Maimoni chapter 4) and the custom in these countries is not to eat honey except that which they bring in barrels from the hive from which they make a drink called mead, and dried figs and dried grapes called roziny (large or small) depending on local custom, for some are stringent not to eat them and some are lenient; therefore they were accustomed in these countries to be stringent not to eat any dried fruits unless it is known they were dried in a manner where there is no concern for chametzing. And tsuker is forbidden to eat it, even to keep it is forbidden (Terumat HaDeshen siman 111). And on the last Yom Tov they eat dried fruits and tsuker kandil that has no chametzing concern (Maharil). And the custom in these countries is not to eat saffron called zafarin or negelach (Maharil}. However they do not forbid its mixture, and so it appears to me:}
mechaber/9:main: A cooked dish that was cooked and barley or wheat was found in it — if they actually split open, the entire cooked dish is forbidden; and if they did not actually split open, the cooked dish is permitted: {Rama: And the custom is not thus; rather they forbid everything in any amount even if they did not split open, and they burn those wheat kernels or barley kernels:}
mechaber/10:main: A cooked chicken in which a split wheat kernel was found on Pesach — it is permitted to sell it to a gentile, for it is not sold at a higher price on account of the wheat kernel found in it: {Rama: And in these countries they are accustomed to burn everything (and see above siman 447 seif 3}. And if it was found on the eighth day of Pesach it is permitted to keep it until after Pesach:}
mechaber/11:main: If a wheat kernel was found embedded in dough or in baked matzah — one removes from it the amount required for removal and the rest is permitted; and there is one who forbids the entire dough or that matzah, and it is fit to be concerned for his words if not in a place of great loss or in a time of distress: {Rama: And so they are accustomed during Pesach to forbid that matzah in which the wheat kernel was found and to permit the others, whether it was found in it baked or raw, and we say "here it was found, here it was." And if it was found in dough they forbid the entire dough — specifically during Pesach; but before Pesach they forbid only the amount required for removal, and so is the custom:}
mechaber/12:main: If they scalded (meaning: they boiled it in water to remove the feathers) a chicken and afterward embedded wheat kernels were found in the water — the chicken is forbidden; and if an embedded wheat kernel or chametz bread was found in a vessel of water and there is not enough to impart taste — for the water is cold — and they cooked a cooked dish in that water or kneaded dough with it, it is permitted; and there is one who forbids if it is during Pesach: {Rama: And there is one who permits even in scalding chickens because we say perhaps it fell there afterward (Tashbetz and Mahariv). And there is one who forbids in other meat and permits in chicken by force of a double uncertainty (Mordechai chapter Kol Sha'ah). And regarding custom it appears to forbid in other meat or in a whole wheat kernel even in chicken — specifically if they scalded chickens, meaning the water was hot; but if it was cold and they soaked the chickens there, one does not forbid from uncertainty. And in a place where one can say perhaps the wheat kernel was digested in the chicken, such as when it is broken (Mahariv}, even in scalding there is to permit by force of double uncertainty; however if the mixtures became intermingled and there is great loss and prevention of Yom Tov joy, one may be lenient in all this regarding rabbinic prohibition uncertainty that is in any amount, and one may permit other cooked dishes that have mixture from that cooked dish of meat that remained in the water or was scalded — so it appears to me:}
mechaber/13:main: If they boiled an acidic pot that is one day old and the (acidic) water descended into a pit during Pesach — it is forbidden to drink its water on Pesach because they became mixed:
mechaber/14:main: If a split wheat kernel was found in a chicken before salting — rinsing suffices; and if after salting — peeling suffices; and some are stringent to say one must peel deeply all around it and cut and discard; and if other chickens were salted with it one peels all of them: {Rama: And some are stringent to forbid everything that was salted together; but the essential ruling is to forbid the entire piece upon which the wheat kernel was found and to permit the others with some peeling; and if one wishes he can sell everything to a gentile as explained siman 447 seif 1, even though they do not customarily do so in other chametz mixtures — so it appears to me:}
mechaber/15:main: A roasted chicken in which a split wheat kernel was found during Pesach — one cuts away the place of its dispersion according to estimation; and there are those who forbid all of it because when one turns the spit the taste spreads throughout the entire chicken; and similarly there is one who forbids all the chickens roasted with it on that spit that touch one another, for through turning the spit it spreads from one to another:
mechaber/16:main: A wheat kernel or barley kernel found in the crop of a bird after they roasted the bird — it is permitted; and the wheat kernel and the barley kernel must be burned, for they are not considered as if consumed:
baer-heitev/1:א: In a river. In the Tur he wrote "and the chametz is not recognizable in them" — it implies that if the chametz is recognizable it is permitted to sell, for the buyer will see and not buy; Taz and Magen Avraham. But the Ran wrote that even if the chametz is recognizable it is forbidden to sell it to a gentile, for we are concerned lest he grind them and afterward sell to a Jew; see Chayei Adam (who rejected the reasoning of Magen Avraham) that since they do not buy flour from the market in a land, in a time of distress there is no concern — for that which is in siman 453 deals with matzah of the mitzvah specifically — see there; and he explains the intent of the Tur that it is a stringency, for even though the chametz is not recognizable and it is only a mere concern, nevertheless we are concerned; all the more so in certainty we are concerned for mishap:
baer-heitev/1:ב: To keep them. And if one transgressed and kept them and planted them in the ground and their growth sprouted — their growth is permitted, as stated above in siman 443:
baer-heitev/1:ג: And one informs him. But one does not rely on the proclamation; Shaarei Gibborim. And when one informs, even many are permitted to sell to a Jew; and even little by little — if he sells to a Jew he need not inform him — Chayei Adam see there. And Taz forbids selling much even when one informs, lest he forget to inform. And if he sold kav by kav it is permitted by force of uncertainty — perhaps he will not sell it to a Jew and perhaps he will eat them before Pesach — see there:
baer-heitev/1:ד: So that it be consumed. Even if you say that also that little amount he will sell to a Jew, nevertheless that little amount the Jew will eat before Pesach; and therefore it implies that orally at the fifth hour regarding a matter where it is impossible that it be consumed before Pesach it is forbidden to sell to a gentile even a little, lest he sell to a Jew; and such is the agreement of Magen Avraham. Nevertheless it appears to me that if grain became chametz for a Jew — much grain on the eve of Pesach and it is in a matter where it is impossible for him to sell to a gentile so that it be consumed before Pesach and there is great loss — it is permitted to sell to a gentile who knows him and recognizes him that he will not touch it at all but guard it for him until after Pesach, and he is permitted to say to him "until you take it," etc., as written siman 448 seif 4; and then there is no concern for anything — Chayei Adam see there. And see Magen Avraham who raised that selling little by little is forbidden in other prohibitions — only here regarding chametz, for there are many uncertainties, they were lenient; and see Chayei Adam:
baer-heitev/1:ה: To a Jew. And if the gentile said to the Jew even one word after he sold him wheat — "these wheats are for strawberries" — it is as written in Yoreh De'ah siman 17 that a gentile is not believed in what he said after he sold them and they left his possession; however, if he is trusted by him it is forbidden — Magen Avraham implies from his words that before he sold them, since they were in his possession, he is believed. And Chayei Adam left it as "this requires further study" see there; and see above siman 453 small seif 9:
baer-heitev/2:א: In a river. And if it is permitted to nullify this grain in the majority or in sixty before Pesach, since it is still a time of permission — the later authorities elaborated on this, and Chayei Adam raised that it is permitted to nullify l'chatchila see there; and see Magen Avraham:
baer-heitev/2:ב: (2) stationary It is not forbidden to drink it, but it is not forbidden to break it because it is a desik in it. The island and in particular Daino is something Durbanan and see HI:
baer-heitev/2:ג: chametzing. And if it had not yet rested the measure of a mil it had not yet chametzed; and if so, even if it occurred on Pesach it is permitted to sell it to a gentile before it rested the measure of a mil — Magen Avraham:
baer-heitev/2:ד: Forbidden. Even if part of them was eaten before Pesach, likewise one may not permit eating the rest; for specifically dry with dry when one of them was eaten, or in three mixtures, there is permission to eat two as explained in Yoreh De'ah siman 110 see there — unlike moist with moist there is no permission in this, and flour is called moist with moist. Bach and Magen Avraham and Chayei Adam see there:
baer-heitev/2:ה: Uncertainty. Taz raised that in a place of loss or prevention of Yom Tov joy, such as when he has no other, there is to permit even in eating see there, and Chayei Adam agreed with him see there. And if a little snow or water fell on grain and its place is known — one scrapes off the upper ones and the rest are permitted — Ateret Zekenim:
baer-heitev/3:_: We establish presumptive prohibition. See above siman 453 small seif 10 from what is written:
baer-heitev/4:_: For ordinary. It is written in Shachnahag that practically he permitted buying wheat for Pesach even though they were stored in pits, as long as we did not see change in their appearance and they are not moist see there. And if there are wheat that sprouted in them — see above siman 453:
baer-heitev/8:א: In barrels, etc., that they make, etc. Explanation: two things are required — specifically from that which is in the barrel it is permitted to make a drink; for even if you say there is a little flour in it, it is nullified in sixty at the time of cooking before Pesach; but those that they bring in small vessels are forbidden even to make a drink from them, and many times it was clarified to me that they mix much flour in them. And to eat the honey in its own form in any case is forbidden, for it comes to be confused; and so too Maharil and Maharshal. And even to make the drink on Pesach — Bach; however honey that they bring with small hives whole as it lies in the hive, not yet crushed — they practice permissively according to all, for there is no way to mix anything in it when they shake them from the hive to the hive; and see Magen Avraham. And Taz wrote that the implication of the Rabbi's words implies those they bring in barrels from the hive — that even to eat it thus in its own form is permitted; therefore it appears to me complete permission to cook on chol ha-mo'ed a drink in honey that is recognizable as coming from a hive, as long as it is fit for drinking on Yom Tov; even though Mo'ach wrote to forbid making the drink on the festival from concern for mixture — nevertheless it appears to me that one who is lenient for honor of Yom Tov in these lands where we have no other drink on Pesach has not lost. See there and see in Shachnahag and Chayei Adam:
baer-heitev/8:ב: Dried fruits. But they are accustomed to make from them a drink — that is, they pour cold water on them and soak them until it becomes a drink; and so testified Magen Avraham that such is the custom in the holy community of Kalish; but one may not cook with them — see there that he elaborated on the reason for the custom:
baer-heitev/8:ג: (3) and Zucker The 19th reporter saw that he came to ask a question before the Elders of the Moharash, the late AP, who stayed in the Hoat Tzokir and ordered to sell it to Akoum Akal. And the 16th and the MA wrote Dain Isor in the OT tzikar or what we recite Kandiil Tzikar for his stay in his house MM used to sell it to the Akoum at first but in retrospect it is allowed and this is the intention of the rabbi in Hagai and Tzikar Kandiil. And not what we now recite Tzikar Kandiil which is more feared and finished sour is that we cook white Tzikar in Yorat pickles and it is not humanized and it is not even allowed to rest because there is a mix of pickles in it. And 40 kinds of tzukar nights in which he hides various fruits and perfumes that have a complete vinegar in them. And the writing of Hai Daff for the beginning should be careful regarding the suspension of these things, if he has passed and stayed those mixtures, and if the PM or preventing the happiness of Yom Tov should not be prohibited retrospectively. We will not be offended by this situation. And before the teacher shoots, a wise investigation is needed as to how and what is done, because this thing changes per the place and per the time, and to begin with, they tend to get worse in every matter, but what we are doing now is Tzukir Kandil, many of the peoples of the land are from Kilin, and they are drawn to this error from the words of the rabbi, and the latter have already agreed that the mistake is in their hands as a mash: Thin, well, there is also a fear of pickles and the drink made from Zukar that Corinne Sharafi or Lat and Ariji practice Get worse and refer to the book of Bnei Haya:
baer-heitev/8:ד: Zafarin. And it is written in Magen Avraham and Tov Ani Keneged Kulam that the way is to soak it in beer and one must seal it in a room or make a partition before it; and if so, the same applies to saffron see there; and see above siman 451 from the law of dyed vessels in saffron that one may not use it on Pesach:
baer-heitev/8:ה: Their mixture. This refers to all that was mentioned above, and even in less than sixty it is permitted. And in tsuker too one does not forbid the mixture even in types of tsuker confections on the festival; and such one may be lenient as written in s.k. 15 see there; however regarding honey Darkei Moshe wrote that if a little of it became mixed in a cooked dish on Pesach one does not forbid it — it implies that if it became mixed in less than sixty it is forbidden. (And see what is written small seif 7.) And such is essential; but in saffron and the rest one need not be stringent even in less than sixty see there; and see Chayei Adam:
baer-heitev/9:_: everything. The cover and the spoon as well as the utensils that were used and the rest of the dishes that we mixed with from the same dish or used with those dishes are all forbidden and this is how the AAG practices the last things, and the 16th as siman 16. All the elders rule to allow the stew even in eating, but it is enough to forbid eating it with pleasure, and refer to the 16th chapter of this chapter and the 15th chapter, and the text of siman 16.
baer-heitev/10:_: To keep it. Because it is uncertainty of Yom Tov uncertainty of chol and mixture of rabbinic uncertainty — therefore we are lenient to keep it. And all the more so regarding noten ta'am le-fegam, for we are stringent on Pesach as written siman 447 — it is permitted to keep it on the last Yom Tov, for it is lenient regarding mixture of rabbinic uncertainty; but in full chametz that is forbidden d'oraisa even on the last Yom Tov it is forbidden in any case rabbinically; and specifically if it was found on the eighth day; but if it was found during Pesach one must burn and remove everything on chol ha-mo'ed; and if it was found on the seventh of Pesach — as written above siman 446 s.k. 4:
baer-heitev/11:א: And so they are accustomed. Levush elaborated to challenge the Rabbi on this, and his opinion is to permit in dough in every matter that is not noten ta'am in cold see there; and Taz concludes that even though regarding other cold there is to permit according to Levush's opinion, nevertheless in dough — through engagement with the dough one compresses the wheat and it chametzs and forbids the entire dough during Pesach if it softened; and so too in chametz bread one should be stringent even in cold, for there is concern for crumbs. And Ateret Zekenim raised thus, and such is the conclusion of Bach and Maharshal see Magen Avraham and Taz. And Chayei Adam wrote: nevertheless it appears to me according to what is written above that if the wheat is not embedded one may permit in benefit on the festival; if so, all the more so here in cold, for the opinion of many decisors is to permit in every matter; and one who is lenient even in eating has not lost, for it is possible that even when they split open one may be lenient in cold on the festival see there:
baer-heitev/11:ב: (2) Heath. F. Damerinan has now fallen into this matzah and has never been in the matzah before. And the Ma'a Dam the Hata was full of water and moistened from the side of Ak, it is certain that it was in water and in the pulp of Ak, all the pulp must be prohibited, and the ma'am is not for a hangman who was swallowed from a place other than water and fell into the matzah. And he wrote further in MA Daha Damri' here it is found here it was because there is no mahezikinan prohibition, that is to say from place to place or from one piece to another, but from time to time in the Hadith a piece of mazekinen is prohibited. For example, if one has a piece of pulp in his hand and a piece of it is left in his hand and a piece of pulp is found on it, they are all prohibited damrinan lest it was earlier and also one should not say faded SS Dashma is not soured, let there be doubt, lack of knowledge, and let there be no doubt, etc. And in the answer of Chez C. M.G. And in the answer of Shabbat Ya'akov, part 2, 17 and 19. In the answer of Maharam of Lublin, 38, he wrote an act of one who took cabbage from the barrels in a bowl and they were taken to another place, and there he found chaff on it. The chaff from before in barrels faded from time to time in Hada a piece of Hezekinan Isor' as a prohibition and refer to subsection 25 of the MA that he wrote and if it was removed to another place and was found by the Amarinan chaff now fell faded from place to place asak to the Madh:
baer-heitev/11:ג: Removal. Even in baked matzah, and even if there are sixty — we require the amount for removal:
baer-heitev/12:א: From scalding. Plain scalding is in a second vessel — a cook. And see siman 447 seif 3 in the gloss. And it is possible here for the reason of pouring coming upon it, and the Mordechai did not read only on account of the bowl; and for practical halachah, if the second vessel is forbidden, for in chametz on the festival they forbid even in cold — Chayei Adam:
baer-heitev/12:ב: (2) in a bubble From the rabbi's point of view here, as above, section 9 to forbid an afi' is not in a koa, it is possible because it is dehaka, since it is more sufficient, lest it later fall out of the whole island, in fact, the 16th Rabbi wrote, according to his method, to prohibit even not in a koa, everything that has been softened, but here it is permissible to sell it to the Akoum, if it is not in a koa dehoy SS, lest we be soured, and lest later it fell, not in a makharinan, but in a haad sika' Chapter 9 Section 9 And the 11th from Kil Afi' in Hai D Section IX to sell to the ACM, refer to Subsection 18:
baer-heitev/12:ג: The chicken. For we say perhaps the wheat kernel was in water at the time of scalding — we do not say "here it was found and here it was," but from place to place or from piece to piece as written s.k. 21; but in one place, such as in scalding where there is room to doubt in time and to say perhaps the wheat kernel was in water beforehand — we do not say "now it fell" afterward. (For the presumption of the chicken is weakened, for it certainly was in water from chametzing agents; and for this reason the cook forbids matzah [baked] in which a wheat kernel was found, and it is uncertain whether it chametzed [while] [still] in dough — if so. And he permitted other matzot. (Chayei Adam) [Taz] see there):
baer-heitev/12:ד: That forbids. See what is written in s.k. 20:
baer-heitev/12:ה: Fell. And such are the words of Beit Yosef: Ravyah wrote in the name of Rashba — if a wheat kernel was found in a vessel in which they rinsed the chicken, we say "here it was found and here it was" — end quote. And Magen Avraham challenged from the words of Rashba himself who ruled that if a wheat kernel was found in matzah they forbid the entire dough and do not say "now it fell"; and he concludes: therefore it appears to me that it deals with where they salted the chicken and afterward rinsed it in a cold vessel and afterward a wheat kernel was found in the vessel, and there is concern that it was in the chicken and was salted with it; for this he wrote that we are not concerned for this, for since the wheat kernel was found in the vessels we do not say that it was in the chicken, for we do not establish presumptive prohibition from place to place; but in matzah it is from time to time as written; and if so, there is no dispute at all — unlike the opinion of Rama — end quote. And it should be said that what he wrote that in matzah it is from time to time as written — it deals with where dough remained in his hand as written s.k. 21, for otherwise it is from place to place — examine this:
baer-heitev/12:ו: Uncertainty. Perhaps now it fell; and if you say it was previously in the chicken — perhaps it was digested — and see Magen Avraham:
baer-heitev/12:ז: (7) The rooster'. And K. MA not exactly chickens, but H.E. meat, daha meiri, here in whole wheat, delikha, digestion. And at the time, Delerboth wrote, he took roosters, even though it is specified in him that the Ha'tim from the hands of a Spika were not sold, and they said, lest later it should fall. And the main thing is per the opinion of the rabbi, as well as the agreement of the 13th and 16th, in particular, if the chetah is not split, the peshitah must be made worse as a shal, and without softening the chetah, it should be eased in every matter, as well as the agreement of the bah and the latter:
baer-heitev/12:ח: (8) Durbanan The apothecary wrote that a piece of sour cream was found in a bucket of water, and it was not known when they took the water from the bucket whether it had sour cream in it or not, and cooked it in it, and we prepared the dish, but the water in the bucket was forbidden because the almsman who brought the water might have put sour cream in it at that time. in a bucket and it was not known if there was chametz in the well at the time he drew to cook from the respondent he cooked in sour water in this he ruled that the stew is allowed but that the water in the separate bucket is prohibited but the stew is allowed because the umbilical cord drawing the bucket gave the chametz at that time but that chametz was not in the well at all. And Tima on the B.I. that I did not feel it and how it would be difficult, meaning that if there was chametz before it was cooked, it would be forbidden and the chametz in the cold is not forbidden and it is possible to use DSL as Rashba DSL also in the cold forbids, but Annan SAL as the Rash and the Tor Dain forbids in the cold and it seems that she sings the chametz in chilled water from time to time to the Dasor, to the day of Dassur, and it is like boiled Akal. and 22 28 and Rashel. An act of one who took a piece of matzah and a piece of chicken in his mouth and ate both together and felt that there was matzah in his mouth and took the food from his mouth and saw matzah and it is not clear whether it was inside the matzah or inside the chicken. He would roll and descend, and from the above mentioned dehamtza is permitted because something is forbidden, they will plead to the voice that was in the hen, and for the sake of Taking the matzah from the same place is prohibited from the state, from the place where the piece was taken, and more above, Dafi' was a piece of meat, as well as a piece of meat that was forbidden from one place to another, and the matzah fell on the meat while it was cold, and so the matzah is also permitted, but if the meat was placed in a bowl and eaten from it, the meat is forbidden, as in the case of a demzeman, for a time from the hezekinen isor, if the dishma was in the bowl at the time the meat was poured into it and two utensils are prohibited. On Passover, and if it is said that the matzah was in the matzah and the matzah was in the meat, lest now it has fallen, there is no doubt. If you say that it was in the matzah, you should forbid the matzah, and this is not the case, Efi' in the prohibition of Durbanan and Efi' in the SAS, and the meat and the matzah are forbidden, per the majority, it is evident whether the goat was cooked or baked with it or not. And who if the bowls moved from place to place when they got cold, they would ask for relief from those who maintain a prohibition from place to place. MA:
baer-heitev/12:ט: That fell. See Magen Avraham and in Chayei Adam:
baer-heitev/13:א: A day old. But if it is not a day old, even the water itself that was boiled is permitted on Pesach, since they boiled it before Pesach and they are not a day old, as explained in siman 451 — Chayei Adam:
baer-heitev/13:ב: The acid. And Bach wrote that even if they became mixed before Pesach in a matter where they were nullified in sixty, and even though it is also noten ta'am bar noten ta'am of the permitted — nevertheless one may not use that water l'chatchila, since it is possible to find other water easily; and so too in Yoreh De'ah siman 95; and Taz wrote: in my humble opinion it appears that here sometimes it is forbidden even b'dieved even before Pesach, even if the sour water remained above and did not become mixed, for they stood and persisted and are as if in their own form; unless he drew from it beforehand several times, for thereby it becomes mixed see there. (And from what is compared to "he did not shake and cover" in Yoreh De'ah siman 92 see there.) And Chayei Adam wrote that one does not forbid b'dieved even though it was not nullified; nevertheless since it occurred before Pesach it is noten ta'am bar noten ta'am of the permitted, and one does not forbid b'dieved see there:
baer-heitev/13:ג: That became mixed. Meaning: even to permit in cold here it is forbidden, since the chametzing substance itself became mixed. And if a wheat kernel or other chametz is found in this pit — it depends on the dispute that the Mechaber wrote seif 12 whether it is forbidden in cold during Pesach; and see above s.k. 20 and s.k. for Mem-Dalet from what is written; and see Chayei Adam. Taz wrote: once a servant brought a vessel with honey called mead to drink, and one wheat kernel was found in it; I said that it does not forbid in cold, even though it chametzed, and even though it is written in Shulchan Aruch seif 12 "and there is one who forbids during Pesach" — we have already proven that we did not find this distinction, that cold does not impart taste at all, and even on Pesach it is permitted; and also there is no concern here that perhaps the wheat kernel was at the hour the honey was boiling, for if so it was already nullified before Pesach from what was expelled from it, and it does not return and revive even though the wheat kernel is still inside it — nevertheless it was cold at that time and does not impart taste — end quote. And it is difficult — perhaps it was soaked inside it from time to time as written in s.k. 30; and it should be said that the incident was on the first night of Pesach — examine this:
baer-heitev/14:א: By rinsing. For cold without gravy is not forbidden according to all, even in chicken where it is impossible without a little moisture — nevertheless in cold it does not absorb according to all, except through soaking a little. (In responsum of Tzitz Eliezer he was stringent regarding a little beer remaining in a vessel and they took water and rinsed meat in it — one may compare it to the law of a wheat kernel salted with chicken; and Chayei Adam struck a spark on this see there.) Or through engagement with dough as written:
baer-heitev/14:ב: Salting. Meaning while he was still salting it; but if it was found after he salted and rinsed, we say "now it fell" — for if it exists that it was on it beforehand it would fall off in rinsing when he rinsed it; and specifically when found on the chicken, but if found inside the chicken it certainly was there beforehand — Magen Avraham; and Chayei Adam wrote that in siman 447 I wrote that pure salted and impure rinsed — also on Pesach there is to permit; and here it deals where the wheat kernel was also salted with the chicken; and I saw meticulous ones careful on Pesach before scalding and salting to open the chicken well or cut it in two and check well lest a wheat kernel be found inside it. And it is written in Shachnahag: one who does so is diligent and rewarded:
baer-heitev/14:ג: All of them. Meaning when the wheat kernel is found on the chicken, for there is room to doubt that perhaps it touched all of them; but if found inside the chicken the others do not require peeling — Magen Avraham:
baer-heitev/14:ד: They are stringent. Because we estimate in all prohibitions salting in sixty — if so, also in chametz it forbids all of it (see Yoreh De'ah siman 105):
baer-heitev/14:ה: The essential, etc. Because he holds that we do not say in rabbinic prohibition that prohibition goes out from piece to piece through salting; and what they estimate in other prohibitions in sixty is because of a definitive matter that we need not estimate between fat and lean — we go with this even to leniency as written in Yoreh De'ah siman 105; if so, also in chametz sixty suffices. And further that specifically in a prohibition where greasiness applies do they estimate in sixty, but not in chametz prohibition where spreading does not apply. And further that where there is another side to permit we rely on his question that he holds chametz is nullified in sixty — and you have no greater side of permission than this, that many gaonim hold that taste does not spread in salting; and one may make a compromise to forbid that piece and no more; and one who wishes to be stringent may decide to burn that piece and keep the others. And if they were cooked without peeling they are permitted, for peeling is only a stringency; nevertheless it appears to me that the piece requires peeling, only the peel does not forbid the piece even though it was cooked with it. And specifically where there is no doubt that perhaps it touched the other pieces; but if there is doubt that it touched the other pieces — by law all are forbidden; and even though we know with certainty that it touched only one of them and we do not know which one it touched — by law all are forbidden and require peeling, for chametz on Pesach is not nullified in the majority; and if so, if it was cooked without peeling it forbids their mixture; for specifically where peeling is only a mere stringency the peel does not forbid the piece, but where peeling is required by law — if it was cooked without peeling it forbids the piece — Magen Avraham; and see what is written in Yoreh De'ah siman 91 s.k. 7; and see what is written above siman 447 s.k. 6; and Taz wrote: since we saw in this law dispute between early and later — Rashal in responsum siman 79 rules to burn everything, and so Darkei Yosef and Bach. And Mishna Berurah disagrees to rule like the lenient and is lenient in the other pieces even without peeling. And Rama in responsum siman 108 wrote: one who wishes to be stringent may decide to burn that piece and keep the others until after Pesach. Therefore it appears to me to practice practically in this manner: if a wheat kernel is found on salted meat dry without brine — one may permit keeping everything; only the place where it was found one peels, and the rest is permitted to keep until after Pesach. But if the wheat kernel is found inside the brine of meat or fish — then it is considered as cooked, for in a small measure it is like cooked in brine or in vinegar, as explained in Yoreh De'ah siman 105; and all the more so if it rested there from time to time — then its law is that everything resting in the brine is forbidden, for it is as if cooked in one pot and requires removal; but what rests above the brine one may also keep until after Pesach, for taste does not spread in brine upward, as explained in Yoreh De'ah siman 68. And therefore what touches the meat in the brine one peels, and the rest one keeps or does as Rama wrote at the end of the seif — to sell everything to a gentile — meaning what is not in the brine; for what is in the brine is forbidden to sell, for it is full chametz — end quote; and Chayei Adam agreed with him see there. And it is plain that all this is when the wheat softened as written s.k. 18 see there. It is written in responsum of Tzemach Tzedek siman 434: if a little beer remained in a vessel and they took water and rinsed meat in it after salting on Pesach — even though water nullifies the power of salt, nevertheless since it weakened it a little and absorbed somewhat, it has the law of a wheat kernel salted with chicken for each of the opinions in this seif see there; and see Chayei Adam s.k. 46. It is written in responsum of Maharam of Lublin siman 91: a wheat kernel placed in a barrel of salted cabbage — the entire barrel is forbidden, for soaked is like cooked see there. And Magen Avraham wrote: and it should be said that it deals where the brine rises above it; and if the brine does not rise above it, it has the law of salting. And so I heard that a wheat kernel was found in a barrel of fish salted for Pesach, and the Gaon Rabbi Binyamin Av Beit Din of the holy community of Poznan commanded to throw that layer into the river and the rest to sell to a gentile — and see Magen Avraham:
baer-heitev/15:א: Split open. Plain for us the law is thus when it softened, even though it is not split open — Taz. And in Shachnahag he wrote: since the Rabbi did not gloss here "even when it is not split open," it appears he holds that when it is not split open one does not forbid in roasting, only the amount for removal see there; but the opinion of other later authorities is not so; and see what is written in s.k. 18 in the name of Chayei Adam and s.k. 24:
baer-heitev/15:ב: Its spreading. And it deals with a lean chicken, for otherwise it spreads and all of it is forbidden as written siman 447 seif 1:
baer-heitev/15:ג: Spreads. Specifically regarding rabbinic prohibition of uncertainty we are concerned for this; unlike other prohibitions — see Chayei Adam and in Magen Avraham; and Ateret Zekenim wrote: and if he does not turn the spit, it appears from the opinion of Rama that roasting has the law of salting — end quote:
baer-heitev/15:ד: One in another. But if they touch one another they do not forbid, and we do not say that absorption goes throughout the entire vessel, as written in Yoreh De'ah siman 92 — there it deals with cooking. And if so, if the chicken is fatty, even if they do not touch they forbid everything — Magen Avraham. Nevertheless when they are not split open it appears to me one need not be stringent — Chayei Adam. It is written in Shachnahag: an incident came to me on the seventh night of Pesach — they roasted two chickens and a barley kernel that is not split open was found in one of them, and I commanded to cut away the place of its spreading according to estimation and throw it away and eat the rest; and they said they were already cut into pieces with the others and do not know where it is — and I permitted everything see there. And according to his method it goes as written in small seif 40; but the opinion of other later authorities is not so as written. And see in responsum of Chacham Tzvi siman 66 and in Shevut Yaakov part 2 siman 17:
baer-heitev/16:_: Permitted. And even peeling is not needed, for the crop is in place of peeling. And Bach ruled to be stringent to forbid all of it. And Taz decided to forbid in eating and permit in benefit; and other later authorities agree to permit completely with scalding; and see above s.k. 36 from what is written. machatzit-hashekel/1:_: In column 20, 20 and 11, lest they grind them, saying that they do not take flour from 5:20, and the rabbinate, which says that the split is evident, it is forbidden to sell them to a Gentile, lest he sell them to Israel, and Israel has no idea to look at them. machatzit-hashekel/2:א: (seif katan 2) For if so, on the eve of Pesach at the fifth hour it is forbidden, for if he sells it then to an Israelite he will not finish it before Pesach:
machatzit-hashekel/2:ב: And they challenged Rava from the mishnah: a garment in which kilayim was lost — behold it may not be sold to a gentile lest he sell it to an Israelite; since the kilayim are not recognizable — the same applies here to these grains:
machatzit-hashekel/2:ג: For one does not buy bread, etc., and for us see below in seif katan 7:
machatzit-hashekel/2:ד: In the incident in Pesachim page 40b regarding a ship of wheat that sank in the river — at first Rava also thought to sell them to a gentile, and Rava challenged him from this baraita of kilayim and retracted and permitted selling little by little as written in Shulchan Aruch; if so he already knew from the baraita of kilayim — how did he err a second time in the incident of stam yayin:
machatzit-hashekel/2:ה: If so, why did he trouble them, etc. Granted, if both incidents did not come before Rava at one time — there is no difficulty why he did not permit in this incident of stam yayin to sell them little by little, for it is possible that at that time this permission did not occur to him and did not enter his mind; for such is the way of people that many times they understand things that previously did not enter their mind. But according to what Tosafos said that at one time he ruled on both incidents — since he ruled in this incident of chametz to sell them little by little, why did he trouble them in this incident of stam yayin and not rule for them also to sell little by little:
machatzit-hashekel/2:ו: And it implies, etc., even one egg — for such is the language of the Gemara and the codifiers: one does not sell an egg of nevelah or tereifah to a gentile — they used the singular egg and not eggs plural. It implies there is no remedy to sell them little by little; and that which they did not give a remedy to grind them or bake them — it is possible that in their place the practice was to eat gentile bread; and then there is no remedy except to sell to a gentile a slice of bread as the Rama wrote at the end of siman 134 in Yoreh De'ah; and it is possible the wheat was abundant and it was not possible to sell so many slices, for buyers for slices of bread are not easily found; and to leave them a long time is forbidden because of spoilage:
machatzit-hashekel/2:ז: And that which the Rama wrote, etc., in stam yayin that became mixed in water — for stam their wine is nullified in six parts water and then it is permitted even for drinking; and if it became mixed in water and there is not enough to nullify the wine — one sells them to a gentile except for the value of the stam yayin in it; and the Rama concluded: however one may not sell much together, etc. — it implies that little he does not have; if so it is proven that even in other prohibitions little by little is permitted:
machatzit-hashekel/2:ח: They will taste the taste of wine. And even so, if an Israelite tastes them he will make a prohibition for the Israelite. This is not so, for one cannot say the gentile will sell it to an Israelite — the gentile knows if an Israelite tastes them he will perceive the taste of wine and the water will return to him, for he will claim it is a mistaken purchase. And even if you say nevertheless we are concerned — nevertheless this taste is forbidden only d'rabbanan, so there is no reason to be concerned for such a distant concern in a d'rabbanan prohibition:
machatzit-hashekel/2:ט: (9) Rather, his intention is that there are regulations in the first chapter of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel's regulation mentioned in tractate 17, page 14, that he should sell everything to a Gentile, except for the amount of wine that was collected in it. A. that a fat of Israel that a Gentile ate without Israel's assistance is prohibited and it is forbidden to sell it to a Gentile in a place where it is customary to eat a Gentile's fet lest it return and we sell it to Israel but cut into small pieces a fet is forbidden to buy from a Gentile. machatzit-hashekel/2:י: For it would be safek sefeika — meaning since he holds that there should be safek sefeika, it is like nullifying a prohibition l'chatchila:
machatzit-hashekel/2:כ: And it requires study, for here it deals with much chametz — for little by little is truly permitted; and therefore what he questions — behold it is safek sefeika — is to permit selling much together. And if so he used the safek that perhaps an Israelite will eat it before Pesach since it is much and will not finish before Pesach; for if it is possible it will finish before Pesach it is called little by little — it appears at first glance that he holds like the explanation of Rambam that if he holds like what Magen Avraham wrote that little by little is permitted — that even if he sells it to an Israelite the Israelite will finish it before Pesach — if so even little by little is not permitted except from the aspect of safek sefeika that perhaps he will not sell it to an Israelite, and even if he sells it perhaps the Israelite will finish it before Pesach; and he holds one may not make safek sefeika in one's hands. Or he holds like the explanation of Rambam that little by little is permitted, for we say he bought it for his own need and will not sell it at all; and according to this, for Magen Avraham who holds little by little is permitted because of safek sefeika — it must be said it is permitted to make safek sefeika in one's hands and he was not concerned for the questions of R' Yom Tov Lipmann that even much would be permitted lest the gentile sell to many Israelites little by little, for it is possible this is not a common safek — that presumably as he bought much together so he will sell it. And see Yoreh De'ah safek sefeika 57 there Shach in seif katan 91 on what the Rama wrote there: safek tereifah — there are those who permit it even though we hold to forbid; nevertheless it is permitted to sell it to a gentile, etc., since there are those who permit; and Shach wrote one may not be lenient in this except in pressing circumstances, for otherwise there are sides to permit; it implies but in another prohibition, even if there is a dispute in the matter, they do not permit selling it to a gentile; and the reason: even though there is one safek that perhaps the main law is like those who permit, and if you say like those who are stringent — perhaps he will not sell it to an Israelite — nevertheless it is safek sefeika made in one's hands and forbidden, for we do not say because it is safek sefeika of a dispute it is better than other safek sefeika; on the contrary, a dispute-safek is preferable to other safek sefeika; rather Shach's intent is because it is safek sefeika made in one's hands, as Rabbeinu Menachem proved in his questions on the novelties seif 2; and he wondered at what Shach wrote in siman 66 seif katan 10 that from his words it implies the reverse — see there; and see Peri Chadash in his questions general 18:
