It implies even if much mixed in a cooked dish it is permitted, since the concern is distant; however in honey Darkei Moshe wrote, and this is its language: however it appears that if a little of it mixed in a cooked dish on Pesach one does not forbid it, for it is fit to rely on the Rosh in such a case, as in siman 447; and regarding rabbinic prohibition in any amount we do not establish prohibition b'dieved — it implies if mixed in less than sixty it is forbidden, and so is essential; but in saffron and the like one should not be stringent even in less than sixty, for the taste of chametz already passed and went, as in siman 447 regarding dry meat, and Yoreh De'ah siman 69 regarding blood:
magen-avraham/9:א: If they did not split open. For since there is a dispute in the Gemara — some say permitted without splitting open, and rabbinic prohibition in any amount — we follow uncertainties to leniency (Rif); it implies if mixed in less than sixty it is forbidden — see Yoreh De'ah siman 98; and Hagahot Maimon questioned: behold in seif 2 he ruled even if they did not split open it is forbidden; and one might say specifically to eat wheat kernels as they are, but to forbid the cooked dish they were not stringent; and it is difficult, since they are lenient only because of dispute, and necessarily they disagree only regarding what descends below, but where they rested at ease all agree it is forbidden — if so why were they lenient in the cooked dish? And one can say: he wrote above it comes to chametzing — it implies they will come to chametzing but are not yet certainly chametz, only uncertainty — therefore they permit the cooked dish; see Tur. The Beit Yosef wrote in the name of Kol Bo: if three barley kernels are found in a cooked dish, presumption there is much and perhaps they split open (Darkei Moshe); and it appears to me they omitted this intentionally in Shulchan Aruch, for we do not hold thus, for the Taz wrote in Yoreh De'ah siman 84 seif 9 in the name of Rashal that we do not say thus except regarding worms that multiply from their kind, but regarding a matter that comes from outside no; and further, one can check if barley is in it; however in a pile of wheat over which rain fell, one can say this reasoning — see there seif 2:
magen-avraham/9:ב: They forbid everything. The cover and the spoon — and similarly other cooked dishes mixed from that cooked dish; and so they practice (Bach); and so the Tur in the name of Rokeach: a wheat kernel found in a pot — the spoon with which they stirred in it is forbidden; if placed in other pots, all are forbidden — end of his words; and so siman 12; and the Taz in Yoreh De'ah siman 92 wrote that if a piece was forbidden from chametz in any amount and fell into another pot, it does not forbid through its release — see there; and he was excessive in his measures that everywhere they practice to forbid; and so Mahari Cohen in Hagahot Orach Chayyim of the Rama; and even though the piece does not impart taste, nevertheless regarding the prohibition it forbids in any amount; and there are ramifications, such as a thing made for its taste is not nullified, and where it is not made for taste it is nullified — chametz within its time in any amount, and after its time in sixty; or regarding if mixed in its species and not in its species — we say it ascended from it as if it is not — end of his words; and so the Bach; and see in the Drisha — nevertheless what he wrote chametz within its time, etc. — explanation: if any amount of chametz mixed in a cooked dish during Pesach and he kept it until after Pesach and mixed from that cooked dish into another cooked dish, sixty is not required, only against the any amount; and it is difficult, for the Bach himself wrote in siman 447 that a thing forbidden in any amount that passed over Pesach is permitted without mixture; and in Sefer Nikudat HaKesef it is written: and if it was intentional — meaning when it passed intentionally it is forbidden; but according to siman 447 even if intentional it is permitted — see there; also what he wrote siman 55 that chametz b'dieved forbids in its species in any amount because it is deishilam — the Talmud Yerushalmi already decided it is not deishilam; and so siman 461 regarding double matzah; also what he wrote dry with dry is not nullified on Pesach because deishilam, and not in its species is nullified in sixty — he did not examine the Mordechai that wrote explicitly the reason: as moist in any amount, so dry; and so Yoreh De'ah, and so Talmud Yerushalmi; and if so even not in its species it is not nullified; and even a piece forbidden because of any amount that became mixed with others dry — all are forbidden:
magen-avraham/10:_: Permitted to keep it. Because it is uncertainty of Yom Tov uncertainty of weekday (Tur); explanation: and rabbinic prohibition in any amount is rabbinic — therefore we are lenient to keep it; but full chametz even on the last Yom Tov is forbidden, as in siman 448; and also Hagahot Maimon who wrote the reason because it is rabbinic — they did not intend to be lenient except on rabbinic prohibition in any amount, siman 447 and Beit Yosef:
magen-avraham/11:א: (1) All the pulp. Zal Hashaba C. Ke6 not only in place A did the khat touch, but here and here through the rolling of a pulp, and Al Baki Ha here is here it was (ASIV) and further that the water in the pulp conducts the coming out of that grain throughout the pulp, they did not say shell but dry in the dry, and even in a place of high moisture like a layer of sap when licked, but instead of a sauce they said that the sauce conducts even something that is not fluttering, and also bread that is in the dough, the bread is made to crumble and mix crumbs in the dough, except that it itself is possible that chametzs others even though it is baked, but my opinion is not inclined to the fact that there will be little that chametzs the whole dough
magen-avraham/11:ב: (2) here is here was Damarinan's interpretation now fell into this unleavened bread and was never in the matzah, and yet if the bread is full of water and moistened beyond that, it seems that it was in the water and in the chametzed dough, then all the chametzed bread must be prohibited. To hang on it as in the same way as in the Gemara in siman 19 and siman 19 wrote and the Ze'al lest it now fall and the atal that was before lest it become sour, and precisely by softening it is forbidden, but in the L.N. everything sheri Akal and Asiv: And Mor'am Lublin 20 in Tash'u' in the A who took a cabbage from the chabi' in a bowl and they took it to another house and there it was found hetah on it and he allowed the cabbage that was in the Damarinan bowl here it was here Akal, but if a matzah is found in a barrel, even the cabbage in a bowl, it is forbidden, Damrianan, lest the matzah was previously in a barrel, and in the SIB in a chicken, and the Omnipresent, whoever has in his hand kneaded it and cut out of it a matzoh and gave it to another person, and a matzah is left in his hand, and a matzah is found on it, they are all forbidden. For the S.A.C., it is always permissible for this reason, and for the L.N., there is no doubt that we will not leave it, there is no doubt that there is a lack of knowledge.
magen-avraham/11:ג: Only the amount of removal. Even in matzah — and see siman 461:
magen-avraham/12:א: The chicken is forbidden. For we say perhaps the wheat kernel was in water at the time of scalding — we do not say here it was found here it was, except from place to place or from piece to piece, as in siman 11; but in one place, such as scalding, where there is uncertainty in time and place — perhaps the wheat kernel was in water before — we do not say now it fell, for so we find chapter 1 of Chullin and chapter 1 of Niddah that we do not say now it deteriorated where there is no presumption; however what the Rabbeinu Yosef wrote in the name of the Mordechai: if a grain of wheat is found in a bowl near the chicken it is permitted because of double uncertainty (as the Rama wrote in the gloss) and not permitted because of here it was found here it was; and one can say: since it is common to find wheat kernels in chickens that eat wheat, we say perhaps it was in the chicken, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 57 we rely on the common — therefore it is permitted only because of double uncertainty — end of his words; Mishna Berurah siman 69 — and it is difficult, for if so even double uncertainty is not, for a common thing is not uncertainty at all, for even for leniency we rely on it, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 57, and so Orach Chayyim HaShalem; rather it must be specifically there it is very common, but a somewhat common thing we consider double uncertainty, as in siman 84; and if so the Mishna Berurah should not have brought from siman 57; and see in the author of the Shulchan Aruch siman 6 in the Beit Yosef that an uncommon thing is not considered double uncertainty; and it appears to me: even though it is common to find wheat kernels in chickens, when they scald them nothing remains inside, especially for Pesach need — therefore it is not called regular uncertainty; and that the Mordechai did not permit because of here it was found here it was, and in the bowl it fell — because the Mordechai holds a second vessel is forbidden on Pesach, as in siman 447 seif 3, and from time to time we establish prohibition; and if you say it was in the bowl when they turned the chicken into it, it was forbidden — therefore he permitted because of double uncertainty that now it is cold and does not forbid — it deals where there was no gravy there:
magen-avraham/12:ב: (2) And there is no point in it. N.L. Dehchi said that the chametz is little and is not unleavened in the water that is in the water S. against it, therefore it is permissible to dakyon Damsho d'rabbanan not mahramin' in the cold, and yet there is Osrin, etc.: and the long clothing is permitted in the cold, etc. that in all the places he passed he saw great and old sages not to forbid in the cold Akal: and therefore the genius from Prague ordered to allow it, but the Maharash of Ostra wrote The Marash of Lublin forbids, as is the practice of most of the world, and in Kraka, and above, Dathloi in the Akal custom, and in truth, even though the clothing is in accordance with the words of the column not to forbid in the coolness of the MM, Mordechai forbade in my shari' flesh, Efi', the sin is found after the shari' s and it is possible to daser to me, that he is in Phili, and in the Kmsh C. Tamz, and so on. The above-mentioned Dabshar Dait Biya Phili is prohibited from the state when chilled, and also if there is any doubt that it is left out of the GAC, it is prohibited from the state, as in the rest of the season, it depends on the custom or per the matter of the time of need, and the Ams of the C.A. Devlehem must be made stricter and the the Omnipresent in the pulp per the fact that the pulp is soured and its taste will be all:
magen-avraham/12:ג: And there is one who permits, etc. It appears from his words he holds the Rabbeinu Yosef forbids in cold even if found after removing the meat and it is not necessary:
magen-avraham/12:ד: (4) The language is not precise, so it is not enough, but the taste is dauki Ahezek, and Amirinan, the shatha fella 22 RIV: And Zel 21 and RiVu Katha in the name of the Rashba, if we find a hetta in the vessel that they removed, the Amirinan hen here is here, it was like a believer, and I do not say, you came from the hen, and so the Law commanded for the act of Akal, and it is difficult. The Rashba ruled that a dam is found in a matcha or a mass. Osrin the matzah or the mass, as the Mash C.A. Hata and it must be felt that she was in the hen and salted with her for that. They didn't feel it and what is the evidence from Momin Damarinan P.O. The inscriptions were found in Momin in the possession of her father Amari' that it is likely that they were there in Momin's possession already before we got married' and if they were found in the possession of her husband, Amari' he was the one who gave birth because the hat was found in a vessel not Amarinan that was in a chicken faded from place to place but in matzah or dough From time to time, as he wrote above, and if so, there is no dispute here at all, yes, I think the main thing is:
magen-avraham/12:ה: By force of double uncertainty. Perhaps now it fell, and if you say it was before in the chicken, perhaps it was digested; and those who disagree hold specifically for impurity digestion helps, not for prohibition, as written in Yoreh De'ah end of siman 83 — see there in Beit Yosef and so there in Shulchan Aruch; and in the Agudah in Bekhorot it is written: even for the answer of R' Meir of Pontremoli one may not permit a wheat kernel in a chicken, for presumably it swallowed it whole and it is not digestion — see there; it implies even if it broke afterward it is forbidden:
magen-avraham/12:ו: And they roasted chickens there. It should read: not specifically chickens were mentioned, for here it deals with a whole wheat kernel that does not require digestion; if so there is no distinction between chickens and meat — if the wheat kernel is found after removing the meat from there, they do not forbid the meat:
magen-avraham/12:ז: That dripped into water. Explanation: even though the wheat kernel was found inside while the meat was soaking in it, nevertheless it is rabbinic prohibition uncertainty, for some permit in cold — therefore one may permit other cooked dishes:
magen-avraham/12:ח: (8) or Nemalg. Pi' and later we found the chaat to the mimer now fell and it was discontinued above SSAV Dassor to eat because of doubt it was enough for us to eat the chaats themselves, but the mixtures of sherry etc. if there is sas in the matzah it is forbidden to eat: and the Bh wrote with one doubt api' to linger is forbidden and api' in HM, and in the sass it is allowed to linger and a matzah is sold to the Akoum and not in the eatable. Gamo' DA dalla mehni indigestion in the prohibition of the Mish'l, and dok' in finished chametz such as bread or pulp, but wheat that is in water is allowed the stew that was cooked in it earlier has been softened SS lest it now fall and the atal fell before lest it has not softened until now and without softening it is not prohibited at all Afi' according to our customs AQ, and according to his words Dafi' in curd is not prohibited without softening according to Act 2 He took a piece of matzah and a piece of chicken in his mouth and ate both together and felt that there was matzah in his mouth and took the food from his mouth and saw matzah and it is not clear whether it was inside the matzah or inside the rooster. It is permitted in the GCC because something is forbidden, they will plead to the voice that he is in a chicken, as in the BID C. K.A., in two cauldrons, there is S. Datlinan in the one that has S. and they are both permitted, and M.M. to take is prohibited from the state from the same matzah from the place where the piece was taken, and also N.L. Dafi' was a piece of meat. While it was chilled, so was the matzah It is permitted, but if the meat was placed in a bowl and eaten from it, the meat is forbidden, as in the case of Demzaman, for a period of time. And so the DM C. 39 and so the meat and the matzah are forbidden per the majority, it is evident if the chatta is cooked, if it is baked, if not, and A. Banda, page 3 of the book, which is found there that runs, meaning that if they cooked a dish in a pot and removed it from the oven to another place and it cooled down, and it is found per the chata damri', it has now fallen out of favor', a prohibition from place to place:
magen-avraham/13:א: One-day-old. And it deals before its time of prohibition (Darkei Moshe); see siman 422:
magen-avraham/13:ב: During Pesach. And the Bach wrote that even if it became mixed before Pesach it is forbidden, even though it is taste imparted by taste of the permitted; nevertheless in water it is not permitted for this reason, for easily he can find water; and so Yoreh De'ah siman 95; and it is possible even the Rabbeinu Yosef agrees to this, only before Pesach it is nullified in sixty:
magen-avraham/13:ג: Because they became mixed. Explanation: even for those who permit cold, here it is forbidden because they became mixed — see siman 447 seif 5:
magen-avraham/14:א: Rinsing suffices. For cold without gravy is permitted to all — see seif 11:
magen-avraham/14:ב: After salting. Explanation: while he was still salting; but if found after he salted and rinsed, we say now it fell, for if so it had been on it before it would have fallen in the rinsing when he rinsed in water; and specifically found on the chicken, but if found inside the chicken certainly it was before; and see Niddah page 3 regarding a box that has rims:
magen-avraham/14:ג: One peels all of them. It should read: the wheat kernel was found on the chicken — there is concern perhaps it touched all of them; but if found inside the chicken the others do not require peeling:
magen-avraham/14:ד: And there are those who are stringent, etc. Because we assess in all prohibitions in salting at sixty, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 105, because we are not expert between weak prohibition and fat — if so also in chametz it forbids entirely:
magen-avraham/14:ה: But the essential ruling, etc. Because he holds we do not say in rabbinic prohibition that prohibition goes from piece to piece through salting; and what they assess in other prohibitions at sixty is because of the matter that ceased, that we need not assess between fat and weak — with this they are lenient, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 105; if so also in chametz sixty suffices; and further, specifically in a prohibition where greasiness applies do they assess at sixty, but not in chametz where spreading does not apply; and further, where there is another side to permit, they rely on the question that chametz is nullified in sixty — you have no greater side of permission than that many geonim hold taste does not spread in salting; and one should make a compromise to forbid that piece, as in seif 11 to forbid that matzah and no more; and one who wishes to be stringent should rule to burn that piece and keep the others resting with it in the barrel; and further one may permit other pieces through benefit by redemption, as in siman 447 seif 1 — end of Rama in responsum siman 128; and so the Mishna Berurah siman 69; and he ruled if the others were cooked without peeling they are permitted, for it is only a stringency to peel them, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 91 — end of his words; and nevertheless it appears to me the piece requires peeling, only the peel does not forbid the piece even if cooked with it; and so is his intent in Yoreh De'ah there, as stated; and examine there that not like the later ones wrote. Also what the Mishna Berurah wrote here even without peeling is permitted — it appears specifically where there is no concern perhaps it touched the other pieces; but if there is concern perhaps it touched the other pieces, by law all are forbidden, as in Shulchan Aruch in Yoreh De'ah siman 105; and even if they know certainly it touched only one and we do not know which — by law all are forbidden and require peeling, for chametz on Pesach is not nullified in the majority, as in siman 447 seif 9; and if so if cooked without peeling it forbids in its mixture, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 69 and siman 98 — see there; specifically in the lower law the lenient prevails, for it is only a mere stringency, for at first they said in the Gemara peeling is not required, only they are concerned lest it absorbed a crumb — therefore the peel does not forbid the piece; but where peeling is required by law, if cooked without peeling it forbids the piece; and with this all the later ones' complaints on the Rama are resolved; and so in the Drisha. And it is written in responsum of Maharam of Lublin: a wheat kernel resting in a barrel of salted cabbage — the entire barrel is forbidden, for soaked is like cooked — end of his words; and it should read it deals where the brine rises over it; and if the brine does not rise over it, it has the law of salting, as in the Rama's responsum; and see siman 447 seif 5; and so I heard a wheat kernel was found in a barrel of fish salted for that purpose, and the Gaon R' Binyamin Av Beit Din of the holy community of Pozna commanded to throw that row into the river and the rest to sell to a gentile; and Mordechai Margaliot further wrote: before Pesach a full crop of wheat kernels was found in salted brine — even though the Rama ruled in Yoreh De'ah siman 105 that chametz on Pesach forbids only the amount of peeling, nevertheless I was not satisfied to permit that chicken, since there was much chametz there, etc. — end of his words; and the Bach's view is like the stringent in salting on Pesach, and so in Shiltei Gibborim; and in Darkei Moshe he wrote he heard in Krakow some are stringent and therefore did not wish to rule on this neither prohibition nor permission — end of his words; and the Mishna Berurah wrote he was in Krakow and did not hear they are stringent on this — therefore; and it is possible the Rama leaned toward that elder author of Shiltei Gibborim:
magen-avraham/15:א: One cuts the place of its spreading. Question: behold he wrote in siman 447 seif 1 and there is no spreading thing, etc. — it implies if there is a spreading thing it forbids entirely; and it should read here too it deals that the chicken is weak:
magen-avraham/15:ב: According to how they turn, etc. It requires study, for it is not so in Yoreh De'ah regarding other prohibitions; and one can say: even though it does not spread much, it spreads a little; and in other prohibitions it is nullified in sixty:
magen-avraham/15:ג: Those touching one another. But if they do not touch one another they do not forbid, and we do not say absorption goes throughout the vessel, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 92 — there it deals with cooking; and if so if the chicken of its species even if they do not touch they forbid everything, as stated; and see siman 491 seif 12:
magen-avraham/16:_: The bird is permitted. For roasting does not forbid more than peeling, and the crop is peeling — therefore one discards it; and the Bach wrote: according to what they practice to forbid in roasting, everything is forbidden — end of his words; and it appears to me in searing all agree it is permitted, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 68; and this is its language of Maharil: one of Maharash — women practice on Pesach to remove the crop before searing it, for they think searing is somewhat close to roasting, and if a wheat kernel is found in it there would be some concern for chametzing; and some are not concerned — end of his words; and it is known Maharil holds to forbid entirely in roasting, and nevertheless he is lenient in searing b'dieved; it is written in Sefer Tanya: all matters of Pesach should not be done through a gentile:
mishnah-berurah/1:א: (1) Grain that was submerged, etc. — in the Tur it is written and the chametz is not recognizable, etc. It implies that if the chametz is recognizable it is permitted both when selling to a Jew and when selling to a non-Jew, for there is no further concern that he will return and sell it to a Jew and he will eat it on Pesach, for the Jew will recognize it; and there are among the poskim who are stringent lest the non-Jew grind it and sell them — however, for our custom that we do not buy flour for Pesach from the market, several Acharonim lean that there is no concern; and in a place of pressing need one may be lenient:
mishnah-berurah/1:ב: (2) And he informs him — but one does not rely on the proclamation, for perhaps there is someone who did not hear the proclamation. And when he informs him it is permitted to sell to him even a large amount; and without notification, even a small amount — it is forbidden to sell to him lest he come to eat it on Pesach:
mishnah-berurah/1:ג: (3) So that it will be consumed, etc. — that is, even if you say he will sell it to a Jew, the Jew will eat it before Pesach; and according to this, on the eve of Pesach in the fifth hour in a matter where it is impossible that it will be consumed before Pesach, it is forbidden to sell to a gentile even a small amount, lest he sell that small amount to a Jew; and nevertheless in a place of great loss several Acharonim agreed that all this is with an ordinary gentile; but a gentile known not to touch it but only to guard it until after Pesach and return it to him, as was explained in siman 448 — a Jew may sell him a large amount of chametzed grain:
mishnah-berurah/1:ד: (4) Before Pesach — and in other prohibitions where their prohibition is not recognizable, it is forbidden to sell to a gentile even little by little; only here where there are several uncertainties they were lenient [Acharonim]:
mishnah-berurah/2:א: (5) In a river — and whether it is permitted to nullify this grain in the majority or in sixty before Pesach, since it is a time of permission — see above in siman 447 seif 1 in Mishna Berurah and siman 453 seif 3 in Mishna Berurah:
mishnah-berurah/2:ב: (6) That water fell on it — and even a small amount; and see in Biur Halacha:
mishnah-berurah/2:ג: (7) Even though it did not split open — behold in seif 9 the Mechaber wrote even though it did not actually split open — that is, even if it softened such that they are close to splitting; and here he changed his language and wrote even though it did not split open, to teach that even though it did not soften at all, nevertheless it is forbidden:
mishnah-berurah/2:ד: (8) For since it rested at ease — meaning, even though regarding sweetness there are poskim who hold it is not forbidden unless they split open, nevertheless according to all we require that they be close to splitting — that case there is different because for sweetness one is engaged with it and does not leave it so much to become chametzed, unlike here where it rested at ease:
mishnah-berurah/2:ה: (9) chametzing — and specifically when it rested the measure of time for chametzing; but if it has not yet rested the measure of time for chametzing, it has not yet chametzed; and if so, even if it occurred on Pesach it is permitted to sell it to a gentile before it rested the measure of time for chametzing; and specifically with intent to eat immediately. A non-Jew who told a Jew after he bought wheat from him that it is for sweets is not believed, even if he speaks guilelessly, since he said this after he sold them and they left his possession; however, if the non-Jew has a presumption of trustworthiness in his eyes, it is forbidden, even if he was not speaking guilelessly:
mishnah-berurah/2:ו: (10) And rain descended — that is, enough that there is room to suspect that much became moist; but if a small amount of water or snow fell on the grain before grinding and its place is known, one scrapes off the upper wheat kernels and the rest is permitted:
mishnah-berurah/2:ז: (11) And a double uncertainty does not help — and see in the Acharonim who agreed one should not be stringent in this except in a place where there is no loss in retaining them after Pesach; but in a place of loss or prevention of Yom Tov rejoicing, one may permit even in eating:
mishnah-berurah/3:א: (12) Dry and hard — and nevertheless if it is known that water came upon them, one must forbid the wheat kernel itself even though its appearance did not change at all:
mishnah-berurah/3:ב: (13) And its appearance did not change — but if its appearance changed or they are moist, it is forbidden even to retain them:
mishnah-berurah/3:ג: (14) We do not establish presumptive prohibition — meaning, and it is certain that water did not come upon them, and it is permitted even in eating. And see in Sefer Beit Me'ir who wrote that all this deals with those ships where the wheat is placed on decks in the middle of the ship and the wheat does not come into the water that the bottom of the ship draws; and also above it is covered — unlike ships (called canal) where the bottom of the ship is known to always be full of water and the wheat is submerged in the water, and also above it is exposed; and it is likely that while it is on the way rain fell upon them, and also when the sailors constantly raise the oars from the water to move the ship, spray certainly splashes upon them from the river water on all sides of the ship — therefore l'chatchila it is certainly forbidden to buy that wheat for Pesach in every manner; and b'dieved in a place of great loss one could be lenient because of concern for rain from above or what splashed from the oars, lest it is only slight dripping; however, because it is known that the wheat placed at the bottom of the ship where there is always water was certainly steeped in them for a long time, only now they dried — they are forbidden even if they did not split open — therefore one must inquire from expert merchants whether they know that if there are sixty against the wheat above relative to what is at the bottom of the ship, it is permitted b'dieved to eat them on Pesach; and if not, they are forbidden even b'dieved. See there:
mishnah-berurah/4:א: (1) There is no fear, etc. - all that do not see a sign of chamitzin per the fact that they follow the majority and the majority do not care, and even those piles that we saw that rains fell on should be lightened in case the rains did not enter except in the upper sheaves but not in the belly of the pile and the atal entered in case they did not have time to miss. The sheaves to be sold and the rain falls on the sacks until the sack is almost completely soaked in water and the sheaves also become wet are prohibited by law during Passover since the reyotah is visible to the eyes and they should be warned by the Omnipresent that the sellers are not strict because most of them are not Torah believers and also we need to warn the grain sellers in a year when there is a lot of rain or water falls on that bag. [HA]:
mishnah-berurah/4:ב: (16) For ordinary wheat, etc. — Knesset HaGedolah wrote practical halachah that he permitted buying wheat for Pesach even though they were held in pits, as long as we did not see in them a change in appearance and they are not moist; and the Acharonim cited this:
mishnah-berurah/5:א: (17) That it dried completely, etc. — Chayei Adam wrote that for this reason the scrupulous are accustomed that all their matzos are guarded from harvest time, for sometimes they leave them attached to dry excessively because they have no time to harvest — and this is what they call shmurah: they harvest them while still somewhat moist. See there:
mishnah-berurah/5:ב: (18) If rain descended upon it — that is, abundant rain; but through slight dripping that descended on the sheaves we are not concerned, and it is permitted even for matzah of mitzvah [Ma'amar Mordechai in the name of Rabbeinu Menachem]; and see in responsa what he wrote in the name of responsum Ma'al Tzedakah:
mishnah-berurah/6:א: (19) Those that are not split open, etc. — and nevertheless one must clarify which are split open, or at least that there are sixty against them:
mishnah-berurah/6:ב: (20) Are permitted — and specifically when they are not moist:
mishnah-berurah/7:_: (21) A Jew, etc. — for it is like chametz upon which rubble fell; and further there is a double uncertainty, lest they did not become chametzed; and if you say they became chametzed, perhaps they spoiled:
mishnah-berurah/8:א: (1) There is no prohibition in it - to say that it is adulterated with semolina that Dahzoki mixed with it, and it is not permissible to maintain it, and even more so if it is mixed with honey, it is fruit water, and it is not sour:
mishnah-berurah/8:ב: (2) and eat it on Passover - some have written, that is, to eat the honey in its entirety as it is, but kneading it into a paste is prohibited because it is found that when removing the wax from the honey, mix water with it, and especially water with fruit juice and acidifiers:
mishnah-berurah/8:ג: (24) However there are those who are stringent — that they are accustomed to mix flour into it for sweetness:
mishnah-berurah/8:ד: (25) Not to eat honey only, etc. — explanation: in this honey that they bring in a barrel from the hive where wax is still mixed in, the custom is to eat it even in its own form, and likewise to make from it a medicinal drink; because there is no manner of forgery; and even to make from it a medicinal drink on Pesach is permitted because of Yom Tov rejoicing if he has no other drink. But what they bring in small vessels cleaned of wax — the manner of non-Jews is to mix flour in them; therefore it is forbidden to eat it, and even to make from it a drink on Pesach. And there are among the Acharonim who are stringent in this even before Pesach, because it is common that they mix much flour in them until there are not even in the water mixtures sixty against the flour to nullify them; and likewise they are stringent not to eat honey in its own form on Pesach even from those that come from large barrels, lest one come to be lenient with all honey [except those they bring with the small rooms whole as it lies in the hive that has not yet been crushed]. And regarding practical halachah in making a medicinal drink before Pesach, it is implied from the words of the Acharonim that they are now accustomed to be lenient even from those in small vessels, for we suspend that the flour will be nullified in sixty [unless it is known that in those places the manner is to mix much flour]; and nevertheless one who is stringent in this not to make a medicinal drink except from honey that comes in a barrel with wax — praise to him. And regarding eating on Pesach honey in its own form from the barrels — it depends on local custom, and in our country the custom is to be lenient; and nevertheless one must investigate and know the local custom, for there are places where they put bread in the hive at crushing time or other chametz matters; and in a place where there is concern for this, the honey is forbidden to eat in its own form on Pesach, but it is permitted to make from it a medicinal drink before Pesach [Chayei Adam]:
mishnah-berurah/8:ה: (26) And dried figs — for there is concern they sprinkle flour on them when they dry them; and grapes are accustomed to dry them in an oven near bread or after they removed the bread from the oven; and there are places where they do not sprinkle flour on them and dry them in the sun — and this is what he wrote that it depends on local custom:
mishnah-berurah/8:ו: (27) Not to eat any fruits, etc. — that is, for the above reason. And nevertheless the custom is lenient to make from them a drink on Pesach — that is, they soak them in water until their taste is absorbed in the water and they drink the water on Pesach; for since there is in them only a general concern, they are not so stringent to forbid even their soaking water; but they are not so lenient to cook them on Pesach in order to drink their cooking water on Pesach, because through cooking their taste is absorbed in the water more than through soaking; and in some places they are accustomed to be stringent with soaking water as with cooking water [unless they soaked and cooked them before Pesach]; and likewise on the eve of Pesach in the name of Noda B'Yehuda agrees that l'chatchila it is proper to be stringent, and therefore it is good to strain the liquid from the fruits on the eve before nightfall — then even if a little flour adhered to the fruits and became mixed in the liquid, it is nullified in sixty:
mishnah-berurah/8:ז: (28) In a manner where there is no concern for chametz — such as if it is known to him that it dried in the sun or in an oven after kashering it:
mishnah-berurah/8:ח: (29) And even to retain it is forbidden — for there is concern they mix flour into it; and the Acharonim agreed that that which we call good sugar, made like a hat, has been clarified through investigation of craftsmen that they do not mix flour into it; and nevertheless they were accustomed to sell it l'chatchila [and b'dieved it is permitted after Pesach, and also on the last Yom Tov they eat it]; and that which has a hechsher certificate from a rabbi from its place of manufacture — they are accustomed to eat it l'chatchila. However sugar made very fine has more concern for chametzing from flour mixtures, and it is forbidden to retain it; and nevertheless b'dieved if one transgressed and retained them, it is implied from Acharonim not to forbid this either; and see in responsa the manner of certification in this regarding eating l'chatchila. And know that in sugar mixtures where they coat types of fruits and spices, and all the more so those made like small balls from sugar mixtures — the Acharonim agreed that one must certainly be concerned lest there is a chametz mixture in them, and it is forbidden to retain by law, and all the more so to eat them even on the last Yom Tov of the diaspora:
mishnah-berurah/8:ט: (30) And on the last Yom Tov — of the diaspora; since it is rabbinic, we are not stringent regarding something that has only a general concern:
mishnah-berurah/8:י: (31) And candy sugar that does not have, etc. — this is not the cooked sugar cut into pieces that we call candy sugar, for in those there is greater concern for chametzing and it is forbidden to retain them and forbidden to eat them even on the last Yom Tov; rather it is sugar that comes from the land of Canada, and it is like our good sugar, and it was clear to them that there is no concern for chametzing at all; and nevertheless on other days they may not eat them except through certification, so that one should not come to be lenient also in sugar mixtures. And the Acharonim wrote that even l'chatchila one must certainly be careful not to retain our Canadian sugar and sugar mixtures; nevertheless if one transgressed and retained them, one does not forbid after Pesach, for there are several uncertainties in this — see Kaf HaChayim:
mishnah-berurah/8:כ: (32) And the custom in these countries not to eat, etc. — but to retain them is permitted:
mishnah-berurah/8:ל: (33) Turmeric — for they forge them with flour to establish its appearance; and likewise they place se'or on it to restore its appearance; and the Acharonim wrote that even turmeric grown in one's garden and guarded from chametzing — the custom is to treat it as forbidden because of appearance, for turmeric is not common in these countries and they will think it is turmeric that comes from distant places; unlike other fruits that were dried by a Jew and guarded from chametzing, where we are not concerned because of appearance, since they are common and everyone knows that sometimes they dry them through a Jew. They further wrote that tobacco — the manner is to soak it in beer in some places, and one must seal it in a room or make a partition before it; and likewise turmeric in places where the custom is to treat it as forbidden. And Chayei Adam wrote that he investigated among craftsmen who make snuff tobacco (that is, they sniff it through the nose) — they moisten the tobacco package with wine, and it is known that yayin nesech is forbidden in benefit by law; and if so it is proper to be careful not to sniff that tobacco all year. And behold all this Chayei Adam wrote in his time; but now one must investigate among craftsmen whether they do so:
mishnah-berurah/8:מ: (34) Or negeliach — because they soak them in barley water before drying them [Darkei Moshe]:
mishnah-berurah/8:נ: (35) However they do not forbid their mixture — since the rule implies even in less than sixty; and this applies to all the above in this gloss; and the reason is that we are not so stringent because of a general concern; however regarding honey and sugar mixtures there are those who are stringent to forbid unless there were sixty in the dish against it; and nevertheless in a place of great loss or prevention of Yom Tov rejoicing one may be lenient:
mishnah-berurah/9:א: (36) If they actually split open — behold in the Gemara there is a dispute regarding soaking barley in water: some hold it is not chametz until they split open from it; and some hold that if they are swollen so much that they are close to splitting, they are also forbidden; and we decide stringently regarding eating them in their own form, for it is forbidden even if they did not actually split open; but regarding forbidding the cooked dish in which the kernels are found, which is only a slight rabbinic prohibition — we decide leniently that one does not forbid until they actually split open; this is the explanation of the Mechaber's view:
mishnah-berurah/9:ב: (37) Forbidden — even in benefit. And also all vessels used with this cooked dish while it was still hot where the hand is scalded in it — they are forbidden to use on Pesach; rather one must set them aside until after Pesach, as was explained at the beginning of siman 447. And if a little of this cooked dish became mixed into another cooked dish, that cooked dish too is forbidden; and likewise if one used with it a spoon with which he stirred in this pot and placed it in another pot while it was boiling — all is forbidden, for since its prohibition is in any amount, we say that here too it releases something:
mishnah-berurah/9:ג: (3) (l) But they prohibit everything - that is, the stew and all the utensils used for the stew, and so on, per the author, in their opinion. And here is the opinion of the 16th in the 16th chapter of Dasur, the stew is even with pleasure, indeed the hai and several other recent ones agreed that in the place of a large loss, one should trust to allow ACP with pleasure:
mishnah-berurah/9:ד: (39) Even if they did not split open — since the Rama's rule implies we do not distinguish whether it is close to splitting or not, because we are not expert in this; nevertheless several Acharonim agreed that at least if it softened we require; and if it did not soften, even if found in hot food, one does not forbid. The Acharonim further wrote that even if three kernels not softened are found in the cooked dish, we do not say that presumably there are more and perhaps they are softened:
mishnah-berurah/9:ה: (40) They burn them — see above siman 446 seif 1:
mishnah-berurah/10:א: (41) Permitted to sell to a gentile — after he removed the wheat kernel from it and only the taste of chametz that the wheat kernel released in the chicken remains; and he may not retain it in his house lest he come to eat it:
mishnah-berurah/10:ב: (2) (Mb) and in these countries, etc. - and where there is a very large loss, the latter agreed to make it easier per the author's opinion, as above, at the head of the Tamaz mark:
mishnah-berurah/10:ג: (43) And if it was found, etc. — that is, even if the mixture occurred from before the eighth day; and the same applies even if one transgressed and retained until this day:
mishnah-berurah/10:ד: (44) Permitted to retain it — because it is an uncertainty of Yom Tov or weekday, and a mixture of any amount is rabbinic; therefore we are lenient to retain it until after Pesach, and then it is permitted even in eating [and some say that even on the seventh of Pesach if a split wheat kernel is found in a cooked dish or in a chicken, one covers them with a vessel until after Yom Tov, and then one eats the cooked dish or the chicken and burns the wheat kernel; and in a place of loss one may rely on this]; and the same applies regarding flavor imparted for deterioration — even though we are stringent on Pesach as explained in siman 447, nevertheless it is permitted to retain it; but complete chametz forbidden d'oraisa — even on the last day it is forbidden to retain it:
mishnah-berurah/11:א: (45) Split open — and for us, if it softened even though it did not split open — and specifically regarding eating; but in benefit one may be lenient in great loss without split open, even without removal of place:
mishnah-berurah/11:ב: (46) The amount of removal of place — for its edge is judged like roast, which forbids the amount of removal; and in dough, even though it is cold, nevertheless we say that through the pressure of kneading something releases around its place:
mishnah-berurah/11:ג: (47) The entire dough — for through kneading it heats somewhat, and the water in the dough carries the release of the wheat kernel that released through the pressure of kneading throughout the entire dough:
mishnah-berurah/11:ד: (48) To forbid that matzah, etc. — and even though the implication of the Rama's rule is that he forbids all of it even in great loss, nevertheless if it softened and did not split open, perhaps one may be lenient in great loss through removal of place:
mishnah-berurah/11:ה: (5) (Met) in which the matzah is found - which is in it when it is baked as a tsal. And we were either the matzah is found in the matzah after baking or when it is still dough after it has been prepared or in a piece of dough, and we do not believe that the matzah was found in the large matzah and was forbidden as a whole, but here it is here it was, that is, that here the matzah is now in this matzah or in this piece of matzah here it was at the beginning when it fell (that is, after the matzah was cut from it, the matzah fell into it) and did not fall If the matzah is filled with water and it is soaked beyond measure, the whole matzah is forbidden, and if it was swallowed from another place, it falls into the matzah, per the matter. The unleavened bread that has the same dough is forbidden, if it was in the same dough before it was cut into pieces. We have soured until now, and instead of a large loss, one should trust to ease, and the above-mentioned MA wrote, since the law is for someone who took a cabbage from a barrel in a bowl and took it to another house or to another place, and there was found in the koa of the cabbage that was in the barrel, it is permissible to keep them from place to place. And here it is found here, the rabbi who left the bowl in the bowl fell, but if the wheat in the bowl is found in the barrel, then even what is in the bowl in another house is forbidden, it is forbidden from time to time, and their strength is from the past. And in any place where there is a large loss, it should be made easier even if it is found in the barrel, even if it is found in the barrel, even if it is found in the barrel, there is a doubt that it has fallen into the barrel now. The time and some of the latter wrote that this is when the wheat is cracked, but if it didn't crack only when it softened, even the cabbage in the barrel should be allowed if there is a lot of loss there due to doubt of sufficiency. And if the cabbage does not come up because of the cabbage, it is permissible to leave the cabbage in the barrel without it being pickled there, only a salty dish is allowed, and it is not forbidden only where it is found, and the rest is allowed according to Mash Ramah in the Hagah in the Sidd. per the Ha Digedas Kvass, which is customary in our country to do on Passover, one must be careful to find out the Yigdas before giving the water Damzoi to find grainin in it:
mishnah-berurah/11:ו: (50) And specifically during Pesach — when chametz on Pesach is in any amount; but before Pesach the taste of the wheat kernel is nullified in sixty; and nevertheless for removal of place one must remove from it, lest it released only around it:
mishnah-berurah/11:ז: (51) Only the amount of removal — even if found in baked matzah, the amount of removal suffices:
mishnah-berurah/12:א: (52) If they scalded, etc. — even though it was explained in Yoreh De'ah siman 68 seif 1 one may not scald even in a second vessel, here it deals that it was scalded beforehand on the feather [Peri Megadim]:
mishnah-berurah/12:ב: (53) The chicken is forbidden — for we say perhaps the wheat kernel was in water at the time of scalding; we do not say here it was found and here it was, except regarding from place to place or from piece to piece, as above in seif 11; but in one place, such as where there is room to suspect in time and say perhaps the wheat kernel was in water previously — we do not say it fell now. And behold the Mechaber wrote here split wheat kernel, and the Rama did not gloss on this at all as he glossed above in seif 9: some say here he agrees with the Mechaber that specifically when split open and not when softened, because there is another uncertainty lest it fell now; and some say the Rama relied on his gloss above in seif 9; and so is implied in the Taz that he did not permit in our matter when softened except in benefit and not in eating; however I found in Beit Me'ir that this law that the Mechaber left in dispute is stated (apart from the view mentioned in the Rama); and therefore it appears in my humble opinion that one who relies to permit in this when softened in a second vessel even for eating has not lost. And if it did not soften, even if the scalding was in a first vessel, it is also permitted:
mishnah-berurah/12:ג: (54) And there is not in it, etc. — the water is cold; meaning, two things are required: that the chametz be minimal such that it does not impart taste in water where there are sixty in the water against it, and also that the water be cold; and therefore we are lenient even during Pesach, for since any amount is rabbinic we are not stringent in cold:
mishnah-berurah/12:ד: (4) (na) It is permissible - if it is known that the wheat has fallen off the surface of the water in water, it is forbidden to soak it as cooked. And even if there is doubt that the wheat has fallen off the surface of the water, it is the opinion of the last ones to make it worse, and if the wheat that is not cracked is only softened, it should not be made worse with the Sika. And even if the wheat is broken, precisely when the wheat is found and then it is cooked in the same water, but if the wheat is found in another water in which it was cooked, the prohibition should be eased, something DAS is that the wheat fell afterwards and the Ethal from before, lest it fall from above the Omnipresent in the water and it is not conquered.
mishnah-berurah/12:ה: (56) If it is during Pesach — those who hold that even in cold it does not impart taste — nevertheless there is any amount; and therefore during Pesach, when its prohibition is in any amount, it is forbidden; and specifically when the wheat kernel was found and afterward they cooked in that water; but if found after they cooked, one should not be stringent in cold because of uncertainty:
mishnah-berurah/12:ו: (57) For we say perhaps, etc. — meaning, since any amount is rabbinic we are lenient in its uncertainty and suspend that it fell afterward; and the same if the chicken is still in the water but the water cooled — we suspend that it fell when the water cooled, and it is permitted according to those who permit in cold:
mishnah-berurah/12:ז: (58) In other meat — in such a case where they left it in hot water after salting and rinsing, and after they took it from there a split wheat kernel was found there — we establish from time to time and say the wheat kernel was there before they took the meat:
mishnah-berurah/12:ח: (59) By force of double uncertainty — lest it was in the chicken itself and was already digested, and chametzing is not applicable to it; and if you say it is not from the chicken, lest it fell now; and the Mechaber's first view holds that even in a wheat kernel that is from a chicken, chametzing is applicable:
mishnah-berurah/12:ט: (60) Whole — for in a whole one we decide there is chametzing, because it is recognizable that it was not digested:
mishnah-berurah/12:י: (61) And they removed the chickens from there — and after the chickens were removed from there they found a split wheat kernel there, even whole; and he cited chickens not specifically, for the same applies to other meat too — one does not forbid because of uncertainty, and we suspend that after taking the meat from there the wheat kernel fell, since the water was cold; and some permit entirely in cold:
mishnah-berurah/12:כ: (20) (Sab) One should not forbid sufficing - but if there was certainly wheat when the meat fell out in the water, one's opinion is that one should act per the opinion. And 27 in wheat but a slice of bread or pulp that is in the water, the latter wrote to forbid even in the cold, because the drowning of the slice of bread and the pulp will crumble and become soluble in the water:
mishnah-berurah/12:ל: (63) And one may permit other cooked dishes, etc. — it implies that that cooked dish itself, even in great loss and prevention of Yom Tov rejoicing, is forbidden with a single rabbinic uncertainty [and see Biur Halacha]; however in the double uncertainty mentioned above it is permitted even without great loss; and all this is in a single uncertainty of any-amount prohibition which is rabbinic; but in double uncertainty of Torah prohibition one may permit only through retention, and all the more so to sell to a gentile but not in eating; and specifically where retention is possible; but if retention is impossible lest it spoil thereby — it is permitted even in eating; and especially where there is certainly a medicinal drink — certainly one should not be stringent:
mishnah-berurah/12:מ: (64) That fell into water or was scalded — it is not in one manner: if the meat fell in cold, even if the kernel is found while the meat is still there, it is also permitted, for there is a rabbinic uncertainty lest in cold there is no release and absorption at all. And was scalded deals when found afterward a wheat kernel in the water after they removed the meat or chicken from there — and it is permitted even if scalded in a first vessel; and the reason is there is uncertainty lest it fell now, and it is any-amount prohibition which is rabbinic — therefore they permit where there is a medicinal drink:
mishnah-berurah/13:א: (1) (Sa) Bat Yoma - And for those who abominated before the time of its prohibition, this is not to abominate a vessel that is of the same day as explained above in the TNAV sign, and the author chose Ben Yomo, as long as the shooter was not a day of the year, even those who abominated themselves are permissible on Passover, since they abominated before Pesach and they are not in siman 20 as explained above in c. And if the abomination was during Pesach, then even if the shooter is not a Yoma woman, the water in the pit is forbidden according to Rama above in the sign Tamaz Si in the Haga:
mishnah-berurah/13:ב: (66) And they descended, etc. during Pesach — that is, the descent was during Pesach, but the hag'elah was before Pesach; and if the descent was also before Pesach, the water was nullified in sixty in the water in the pit; and there are those who are stringent that even if there are sixty against them, one may not use that water l'chatchila, since one can easily find other water. Forbidden to drink its water — and if one transgressed and cooked from them a cooked dish, Peri Megadim wrote one may permit if it is great loss, since the hag'elah was before Pesach:
mishnah-berurah/13:ג: (67) Because they became mixed — explanation: even for those who permit in cold above because it does not impart taste at all — nevertheless here it is forbidden because through becoming mixed, behold the body of chametz is mixed in it. If grain kernels are found in a water well on Pesach, the Acharonim wrote it is proper to be careful in everything possible not to use that water on Pesach even for those who permit in cold, lest it was pickled in it from the outset and is like pickled; and nevertheless if he has no other water, since his life depends on it, one may permit because of double uncertainty — lest it fell now; and if you say it fell from the outset previously, perhaps it did not split open and soften until within the outset and did not become pickled from when it became chametz; and we rely on the poskim that cold does not forbid without pickling. And a slice of bread found in a well — see above in note 62. One who wishes to draw on Pesach from wells of non-Jews or from wells of Jews not guarded from chametz all year — it is proper that he strain the water through a clean garment each time he draws:
mishnah-berurah/14:א: (68) Split wheat kernel — see in Biur Halacha that for us this seif applies even when only softened:
mishnah-berurah/14:ב: (69) Rinsing suffices — for cold without gravy, according to all it does not forbid; and even if the chicken was rinsed, nevertheless since the wheat kernel was not steeped in water it does not forbid; and nevertheless rinsing is required, and one may not rely on the rinsing they rinse after salting:
mishnah-berurah/14:ג: (70) Peeling suffices — and nevertheless peeling is required even though it is cold, for we rule salting is like boiling and it absorbs the moisture of the wheat kernel into the meat to the depth of peeling. And all this when found while still salting on it; but if found after it was salted and rinsed, we say it fell now, and rinsing alone suffices; for if it had been on it previously it would have fallen during rinsing when they rinsed the meat in water. And specifically when found on the chicken externally; but if found inside the chicken, presumably it was previously, even at salting time, and what prevented it from falling during rinsing was that the chicken's edges held it back:
mishnah-berurah/14:ד: (71) And there are those who are stringent to say one deepens — meaning, not like the first view that it suffices to peel the meat around the place of the wheat kernel alone; rather one deepens all around it and cuts; and the reason is since on Pesach its prohibition is in any amount, we say something spreads in all the surroundings of the place of the wheat kernel:
mishnah-berurah/14:ה: (72) He peels all of them — and it deals when the wheat kernel is found on the chicken, for there is room to suspect lest the wheat kernel touched all of them; but if found inside the chicken, the others do not require peeling:
mishnah-berurah/14:ו: (73) And there are those who are stringent to forbid all, etc. — because we are stringent to forbid in all prohibitions in salting in sixty [because we are not expert between weak prohibition and fat prohibition] — evidently it spread throughout; if so, automatically in chametz whose prohibition is in any amount, it forbids all of them:
mishnah-berurah/14:ז: (74) But the essential view — because those hold we do not say in any-amount prohibition which is rabbinic that it goes out from piece to piece through salting; in chametz which is weak, they were stringent only at the measure of sixty to forbid from piece to piece even in weak, and not in any amount. And further that specifically in a prohibition where fat applies do we estimate weak even at sixty, because we are not expert between weak and fat, and we say it spreads until sixty — unlike chametz where spreading is not applicable at all, and our judgment is if we are stringent to forbid that entire piece:
mishnah-berurah/14:ח: (75) Through some peeling — and this is in a manner where there is room to suspect lest the wheat kernel touched them too, as above in note 72; and even if we know for certain it touched only one of them and we do not know which one it touched — all require peeling, for chametz on Pesach is not nullified in the majority, as written siman 447 seif 9; and if they were cooked without peeling, their mixture is forbidden:
mishnah-berurah/14:ט: (9) (o) To sell everything, etc. - refer to AR, whose opinion the Dharma is not Kai, I will only leave pieces, but that piece with the goat on it is not allowed to be sold, per the Haga above in the SKI, and the last remaining parts mean that it is only by Maliha McKilinan to sell that piece, and only if he peels the skin from the meat where the goat is on it:
mishnah-berurah/14:י: (77) To a gentile — see in the Taz who wrote he ruled practically that the same applies: permitted to retain the other pieces until after Pesach, since they are only uncertainty of contact; and also that piece one may retain, only that in it one must peel first the place of the wheat kernel; and from the words of Magen Avraham it is implied that his view is like the Rama's view that that piece is forbidden to retain; and it appears that when softened and did not split open, one may rely on the words of the Taz; and Kaf HaChayim agrees to the words of the Taz:
mishnah-berurah/14:כ: (20) (Eh) As Mishak C. Tamaz, etc. - TS he and Tsal A'G Dain practice the same way in other mixtures of chametz as Mashak, the sign of Tamaz SA and its meaning is explained by swallowing something of chametz. No one else can sell the chametz fee here by salting it. It is recognized by the Akoum when one finds hatta on salted meat during the salting or after salting and removing and salting a second time in the pot and finding hatta on the meat without stock, but if the hatta is found inside the stock, then consider everything as cooked with a small amount of fat, it is occupied by stock, then everything that is placed in the stock must be prohibited and should be in the skin, but what is placed above the stock should be done as Rama Dabzir wrote. Until after Pesach, and as we wrote above in the 16th Da'at, and also if wheat is found placed in a barrel of salted cabbage, the whole barrel is forbidden as cooked, and precisely when the stock rises, the stock is not salted, and it is ruled as above in Sec. Even without a peel, from the principle of the law, even though the water was forbidden because of the reward that would interfere with it from anywhere, the meat did not swallow any of this water because it was chilled, and even though the meat was still salty when it was boiled and the salt was boiling from everywhere, he did not swallow any of the water, since the water they were boiled in cancels the strength of the salt and it does not have the power to swallow the water in the meat. These are the opinions of Ha Damdina that the meat should have a rind, since it is a fish dish and the meat is not even salted at all:
mishnah-berurah/15:א: (1) (a pen) that is in it, etc. - wrote the HC Dr. Ral. Indeed, what is in it is a dish for horses that has soured in the water in which it was washed, but if it is on the chicken, if it is discolored during washing, it would fall, and now it has fallen, and the chicken's fat is like fruit and does not miss:
mishnah-berurah/15:ב: (2) (f) Cracked wheat - and per the Rama's words above in Set 55, it was not even cracked, only softened, but not softened at all:
mishnah-berurah/15:ג: (81) One cuts the place of its spread, etc. — that is, as written above that one deepens all around it; for in roast, according to all, one must be stringent more; and specifically if the chicken was lean; but if it is fatty, at the place of contact of the wheat kernel the whole thing is forbidden, for the permitted part goes and seasons the wheat kernel, and afterward the wheat kernel releases something throughout the entire chicken:
mishnah-berurah/15:ד: (82) Because when they turn over, etc. — and specifically in chametz prohibition which is in any amount we are concerned for this, unlike other prohibitions:
mishnah-berurah/15:ה: (5) (Peg) the shpod - means a dam roasted over coals. It is not allowed to burn more than it is, and in the opinion of the above mentioned rabbi, it is certainly permissible to lighten the roast more than to salt it [last]:

And I wonder greatly at the words of the rabbi, for the Rambam holds that one must inform him, and for him it is truly permitted even a large amount, as he states here explicitly; and the Tur's difficulty is according to his reading that reads to Israelites — therefore he questioned even a large amount; but according to what the Maggid said that the Rambam's version does not read to Israelites — the Tur's difficulty is resolved, for if so the large amount is also permitted to an Israelite, only that Rava teaches us that even for a gentile, where informing is not applicable, nevertheless one sells to him measure by measure; and it appears that one should be concerned for the Tur's reading, which is the reading of most books — namely to Israelites, and it is not permitted except with informing; and nevertheless one should not sell except a little, for the reason that when he sells a large amount and will rely on the informing there is concern lest he forget to inform one of the buyers and a stumbling block will come — unlike when he sells a little to a gentile, where there is a double uncertainty that perhaps he will not sell it to an Israelite; and if you say he will sell it to him, perhaps he will eat it before Pesach, as stated above — for practical halachah:

turei-zahav/8:א: There are those who are stringent. It is the Mordechai that we are concerned lest flour or fine flour was mixed in. And the Beit Yosef wrote that there is no prohibition in this, for it is fruit juice and only fine flour chametzs; and it is possible that they are concerned that it is full chametz since they knead wheat first. And the Rosh wrote in a responsum general 24 that he did not see a custom of prohibition in honey, for mixing flour is not common and also it was nullified before Pesach; and if we come to be concerned because of mixtures we should forbid it all year — some say they put nevelah meat into it and it turns into honey and is permitted, for after the fact we follow — end of his words. And nevertheless the Rama concludes that one may not eat it on Pesach except what they bring from the hive, even though in the Mordechai he forbids this too because of substitution with other honey — it is an extra stringency. And I saw in many places that they eat it, and also in the holy community of Krakow there is no custom to forbid — unlike the Rama's words here that one should not eat honey except what they bring from the hive that they make a drink from, etc. — meaning even to eat it as is it is permitted, for they make a drink from it l'chatchila; but one should not say that specifically the drink is permitted because it was made before Pesach, for he did not mention before Pesach; and further, he began with eating — therefore this too even in eating is permitted, only that he mentioned the drink as evidence that people practice leniency. And based on this it appears to me there is full permission to cook on chol ha-mo'ed a drink called mead from honey that is recognizable as coming from the hive to the sight of people — anything fit for drinking on Yom Tov; even though the author of the Or Zarua wrote to forbid making the drink on the festival because of concern for mixtures, and wrote that so they practiced — nevertheless it appears to me that one who is lenient for the honor of Yom Tov in these countries where we have no other drink on Pesach has not lost; and there is no applicable custom of prohibition here, for each one prepares for himself before Pesach; but if one comes to cook on the festival and has no drink other than that — one should not protest him, and honoring Yom Tov is in his hand, as appears to me. And based on the words of the Rosh's responsum that we mentioned in the name of R' Yonah, it appears to teach merit on what is written in Shulchan Aruch Yoreh De'ah siman 114 that the Rashba was careful from saffron because they mix dry meat in it; and according to R' Yonah's words there is permission since the saffron dissolves in food and the prohibition is nullified, and it is literally like honey here all year:

turei-zahav/12:ה: By force of double uncertainty. The author of the Or Zarua questioned that this is not double uncertainty, for the mind of fools is not a mind, and it is possible that one who is expert knows to assess that it was not digested; and I do not know the difficulty, for this matter cannot be known — it is like entities in a full stomach; and all such cases are certainly uncertainty, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 81. And one can say: here in this seif regarding grain on top he wrote the Rama that one may not permit for eating because of double uncertainty; and one should not say here there is another leniency that there is only rabbinic prohibition in any amount, but regarding grain there is uncertainty in all the grain — this is not so, for above too in some places it implies the majority is permitted; and so is the law in that very responsum of the Rashba that the Beit Yosef brings in a year when rains were abundant — what is written in Shulchan Aruch seif 4, and there it is explained that the majority is permitted; and further, wherever double uncertainty helps, it helps even for d'oraisa prohibition; and therefore it appears he was stringent there for eating only because there is possibility without loss — it is like a matter that has permitters; and as the author concluded in that law that we copied in seif 2, concluding: since there is no loss in keeping it, etc. — unlike food needed for Pesach, where we follow practical halachah, as appears to me. Rokeach wrote: a piece of chametz was found in a bucket of water and it was unknown when they took the water from the bucket whether chametz was in it or not, and they cooked in it and they poured out the cooked dish — but the water in the bucket is forbidden, for perhaps the gentile who brings water put chametz in at that hour — end of his words; and the Beit Yosef brought these words and they have no explanation; and it appears there is an error, and it should read: when they took water from the well — the intent is they drew water first from the well to cook, and afterward drew water in a bucket and chametz was found in the bucket, and it was unknown whether chametz was in the well when they drew to cook — automatically they cooked in chametz water; with this he ruled the cooked dish permitted, but the water in the bucket alone is forbidden, for the gentile drawing to the bucket put chametz at that hour, but that chametz was not in the well at all. And it is astonishing on the Beit Yosef who copied and did not notice; and how can it be — difficult, for it implies if the chametz was before it was cooked it would be forbidden, but chametz in cold does not forbid, as above; and it is possible he holds like the Rashba that the Beit Yosef brings, who argues on the Rosh and holds cold also forbids, and we hold like the Rosh and Tur that cold does not forbid; and it appears if chametz soaked in cold water from the eve — forbidden to all, for soaked is like cooked; and so the author of the Or Zarua in the name of Rashal. The Tur wrote, and this is its language in Sefer Rokeach: a wheat kernel found in a pot — the spoon with which they stirred in it is forbidden; if he placed it in another pot, all are forbidden; and the Beit Yosef on this: it is simple, and why did he not copy it in Shulchan Aruch? And I say this requires deep study, for at first glance this passage is not halachah, for the Talmud Yerushalmi siman 93 in the name of Rabbeinu Tam wrote: what is forbidden in any amount does not impart taste, and any amount from it does not forbid in any amount afterward — meaning from what it releases; and as the Tur wrote there: even if forbidden in its species in any amount — for R' Yehuda we do not say two any-amounts; and if so here, where the spoon forbidden from the pot containing a wheat kernel is forbidden because of any amount — why should it forbid another pot in any amount? And so in the Levush siman 92: chametz and yeast forbidden in any amount do not impart taste, and if it fell again into another pot it is nullified in the majority if unrecognized, and if recognized one discards and the rest is permitted — end of his words; and there we wrote that this if unrecognized nullification is not the intent, and they said this only when recognized one discards; and its release is not forbidden in any amount since it itself was forbidden in any amount; and if so this case here is very difficult; and it appears to me to answer properly: here with the spoon we are concerned lest the spoon touched the wheat kernel itself in the pot and was forbidden from it, not from the cooked dish in the pot. And we find such in Yoreh De'ah siman 95 regarding bowls washed in a dairy churn — they forbid there because the bowls touch the griddle and receive taste from it, and we do not follow the water in the griddle; here too the spoon receives from the wheat kernel itself; and one should not say here as well that the way of the spoon is to touch everything in the pot when stirring, and it was forbidden by taste imparted, not by any amount, for there had to be sixty in what was absorbed in the spoon against the wheat kernel; and it is possible there is not so much absorption, even though we assess the whole spoon everywhere — that is for stringency to assess against it because we do not know how much comes out, but for leniency no, for perhaps there is not so much absorption that there would be sixty in it against the wheat kernel — therefore it properly forbids (but if one inserts) another spoon into that pot that was forbidden because of inserting the first spoon — that spoon is not forbidden so as to forbid another pot when they insert it, since it is forbidden only in any amount from the cooked dish, it does not forbid others in any amount; and similarly if they removed the wheat kernel from the pot it fell in and someone inserted a spoon — it does not forbid afterward by insertion into another pot in any amount, unless there is sixty against the spoon, and it is permitted, as appears to me clearly; and this is a peg that will not move in seif 4:

turei-zahav/14:א: One peels all of them. In responsum of the Mishna Berurah siman 69 he disagrees on this, that peeling is not required for the rest, for if because of concern lest they touched the wheat kernel itself we do not establish prohibition except here it was found here it was; and he expanded somewhat on this. And it is astonishing on him that he did not examine Shulchan Aruch in Yoreh De'ah siman 105 seif 9 that wrote there: and if it is unknown whether milk touched all of them, all of them, etc. Further difficulty: here peeling is not required at all, since the wheat kernel does not spread at all like a weak thing; and he expanded that we are not stringent on chametz on Pesach to say it spreads. And certainly this is true, as we mentioned in siman 461 seif 4 regarding adhesion to matzah — only that case is different, for there is nothing that spreads entirely, unlike when there is meat that spreads — we are concerned lest it went and seasoned the wheat kernel and it returns to spread in the meat, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 98 seif 5; and even a thin piece of prohibition and the permitted of its kind, etc. — we can say here too with matzah and meat; but I already cast a stone on this passage in Yoreh De'ah there. And I mentioned Rashal's words that in salting at least we do not say this reasoning; and nevertheless peeling is required even for the rest because of concern for contact, as stated; and in that responsum he mentioned there that wherever peeling is required and not possible it is permitted like Ra'avad's view. turei-zahav/14:ב: And there are those who are stringent. The reason we hold in all prohibitions salting is like cooking — so too regarding chametz; and the Rama decided to be lenient in the other pieces, since also in other prohibitions it is only a stringency of the custom that peeling suffices in salting according to most poskim; and therefore on chametz on Pesach, which is rabbinic prohibition in any amount, one may be lenient; and it would have been fit to be lenient even in that piece that peeling should suffice; only since we see the wheat kernel and it rests on it, one should be stringent on it like the stringent ones; and there is an error in what he wrote, etc. — and it should read to sell everything to a gentile, even though we do not practice thus in other chametz mixtures, as in siman 447; and he means that here in salting it is more lenient than other chametz mixtures mentioned in siman 447. And for the law we saw dispute among the early ones in the Mordechai chapter 20 whether to forbid in salting like cooking; and the later ones — Rashal in responsum siman 79 — rule to burn everything, and so too the author of She'erit Yosef and the author of the Or Zarua. And the Mishna Berurah disagrees with him to rule like the lenient ones, and he is lenient in other pieces even without peeling; and the Rama in responsum siman 128 wrote to permit other pieces, and this is its language: even one who wishes to be stringent should rule as he heard some sages instruct to burn that piece and keep the others after Pesach; and in my humble opinion one should practice thus: if a wheat kernel is found on salted dry meat without brine, one may permit keeping everything this way — where it was found one peels, and the rest one keeps, since there is only uncertainty of contact and one does not eat from it on Pesach but keeps it for after Pesach; and this certainly has no stumbling block, since for many great early and later authorities it is eaten, and we do not keep it; but if the wheat kernel is found inside the brine of meat or fish, then it is considered like cooked, and all the more so if it rested there from the eve — its law is as all that rests in the brine is as if cooked in one pot and all is forbidden and requires destruction, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 105 regarding soaked in brine or vinegar that in a small measure it is like cooked; but what rests above the brine one may also keep until after Pesach, for spreading does not go upward in brine, as explained in Yoreh De'ah seif 9 that there is no spreading upward in brine; and therefore what touches the meat in the brine one peels, and the rest one keeps or does as the Rama wrote at the end to sell everything to a gentile; and it appears here too one should peel the place of the wheat kernel first, for this is full chametz, as appears to me; and this is when it is not in the brine, but if it is in brine it is forbidden to sell, for it is full chametz, and one should do as written nearby. And what Shulchan Aruch wrote in this seif: if an embedded wheat kernel is found — it is plain that for us the law is thus if it softened, even though it is not embedded, as stated:
turei-zahav/16:_: The bird is permitted.
